title: Incentive stock options (ISOs)
summary: Incentive stock options (ISOs) are a type of employee stock option that can qualify for favorable tax treatment under IRC Section 422. Unlike NSOs, ISOs generate no ordinary income at exercise - instead, the spread at exercise is an AMT preference item, and qualifying dispositions are taxed at long-term capital gains rates.
text: ## What ISOs are and why they exist Incentive stock options are a form of equity compensation authorized by Congress in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 and now governed by IRC Section 422. Congress created a preferential tax structure for ISOs to encourage broad employee ownership and long-term investment in employer stock. The core tax benefit is straightforward: employees who receive ISOs and satisfy specific holding requirements pay capital gains rates on their eventual profit, rather than the ordinary income rates that apply to most compensation. ISOs can only be granted by corporations (not partnerships or LLCs taxed as partnerships) to their employees - directors and independent contractors are ineligible. The option must be granted under a written plan approved by stockholders within twelve months of the plan's adoption, and it must specify the aggregate number of shares that may be issued and the class of employees eligible to receive grants. ## Key statutory requirements under IRC § 422 For an option to qualify as an ISO, it must satisfy each of these requirements at grant: **Exercise price at or above FMV.** The exercise price must equal or exceed the stock's fair market value on the grant date. For companies whose stock is not publicly traded, this generally requires a Section 409A valuation. For more than 10% stockholders, the exercise price must be at least 110% of FMV. **Ten-year maximum term.** The option may not have a term exceeding ten years from the grant date. For 10%-or-more stockholders, the maximum term is five years. **$100,000 annual vesting limit.** Based on grant-date FMV, no more than $100,000 worth of ISOs may first become exercisable in any calendar year per employee. Amounts exceeding this limit in a given year are automatically reclassified as NSOs. **Non-transferability.** ISOs cannot be transferred other than by death. The option must be exercisable only by the employee during the employee's lifetime. **Employment requirement.** The option must be exercised while the employee is employed by the corporation (or a parent or subsidiary) or within three months of termination, except in cases of death (where the period extends to 12 months) or disability. ## Tax treatment: the qualifying disposition The ISO's key tax benefit materializes only when a qualifying disposition occurs. A qualifying disposition requires two simultaneous holding periods: - The shares must be held more than **two years** from the grant date, and - The shares must be held more than **one year** from the exercise date. When both tests are met at sale, the entire gain from the original exercise price to the sale price is treated as long-term capital gain. No ordinary income arises at grant or at exercise. **Example:** An employee receives an ISO with a $10 exercise price when the stock trades at $10. Four years later, she exercises when the stock is at $40. Two years after that, she sells at $60. She has no ordinary income at grant, no ordinary income at exercise, and reports a $50 long-term capital gain ($60 sale price minus $10 exercise price) in the year of sale. ## Disqualifying dispositions A disqualifying disposition occurs when shares acquired through ISO exercise are sold or transferred before satisfying the holding periods. Common triggers include selling within one year of exercise, giving shares away, or selling in the same year of exercise. When a disqualifying disposition occurs, the employee must include ordinary income equal to the lesser of: (a) the FMV of the stock on the exercise date minus the exercise price, or (b) the amount realized on sale minus the exercise price. This ordinary income is reported by the employer on Form W-2 and must be included in wages for payroll tax purposes in the year of the disqualifying sale - not the year of exercise. Any gain above the ordinary income component (i.e., sale price minus FMV at exercise) is capital gain, with the holding period determined by how long the shares were actually held from exercise to sale. ## The AMT complication The most significant administrative complexity for ISOs is the alternative minimum tax. Under IRC § 56(b)(3), when an employee exercises an ISO and does not sell the shares in the same calendar year, the spread at exercise (FMV minus exercise price) is an AMT preference item. This amount is added to the employee's alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI) and may trigger AMT liability in the exercise year. The AMT credit mitigates this over time: AMT paid because of ISO exercises generates a minimum tax credit under IRC § 53 that can offset regular tax in subsequent years when regular tax exceeds the tentative minimum tax. However, the credit cannot create a refund, so it may take several years to fully utilize. Plan administrators should inform employees that early in each year, before stock prices move significantly, is often the lowest-AMT-risk time to exercise ISOs. Employees with large unrealized spreads should be directed to a tax advisor to model AMT exposure before exercising. ## Post-termination rules After an employee terminates, ISOs must be exercised within three months to retain their ISO character. If the exercise window in the stock option agreement is longer (for example, many plans give 90 days but some give up to 10 years for vested options), options not exercised within three months of termination convert to NSOs. The administrator should track termination dates carefully and notify departing employees of this deadline in their termination documentation. For disability terminations, the post-termination exercise window extends to 12 months. For death, the estate or beneficiaries have 12 months following the date of death. ## Form 3921 reporting Corporations must file IRS Form 3921 for each employee who exercises an ISO during the calendar year. The form reports the grant date, exercise date, exercise price, FMV at exercise, and the number of shares transferred. This form is due to the IRS by February 28 (paper) or March 31 (electronic) of the following year, and a copy must be furnished to the employee by January 31. Failure to file carries penalties under IRC § 6722.

title: Non-qualified stock options (NSOs)
summary: Non-qualified stock options (NSOs) are the most flexible form of stock option, available to employees, directors, consultants, and other service providers. The spread at exercise is ordinary income subject to payroll taxes, and the company receives a corresponding tax deduction. NSOs carry none of the statutory restrictions that apply to ISOs.
text: ## What makes an option non-qualified An NSO is any stock option that does not satisfy all of the statutory requirements for ISO treatment under IRC Section 422. This encompasses both options granted without any intent to meet ISO requirements and options that would otherwise qualify as ISOs but fail one or more of the statutory tests - such as options granted to non-employees, options with exercise prices below FMV, or options that exceed the $100,000 annual limit. The word "non-qualified" does not mean the option is deficient in any ordinary sense. It means only that the option does not qualify for the special tax treatment Congress reserved for ISOs. In practice, NSOs are far more common than ISOs in aggregate grant volume because they can be issued to a broader class of recipients and carry no statutory design constraints. ## Tax timing: grant versus exercise For most NSOs, there are two possible points of taxation to consider: the grant date and the exercise date. **At grant:** Under Treasury Regulation § 1.83-7(a), an NSO is taxable at grant only if it has a "readily ascertainable fair market value" at the time of grant. An NSO has a readily ascertainable FMV only if the option itself is actively traded on an established market - an uncommon situation. Options granted by private companies and most public-company options not separately traded do not have readily ascertainable FMV and are therefore not taxable at grant. **At exercise:** For the vast majority of NSOs, the taxable event is exercise. When the option holder exercises, the spread - the excess of the stock's FMV on the exercise date over the exercise price - is ordinary compensation income under IRC § 83(a). This income is subject to federal income tax at ordinary rates and is also subject to FICA taxes (Social Security up to the annual wage base and Medicare without limit, plus the additional 0.9% Medicare surtax for high earners). **After exercise:** Post-exercise, the holder owns stock with a cost basis equal to the exercise price plus the ordinary income recognized. Any subsequent appreciation from exercise-date FMV to sale price is capital gain. The character (short-term or long-term) depends on how long the shares are held after exercise. ## Withholding obligations for employers When an employee exercises an NSO, the employer must withhold income taxes on the spread under IRC § 3402(a) and must withhold and remit FICA taxes. The employer has several mechanisms to satisfy this obligation: - **Net share withholding (sell-to-cover):** The broker retains a portion of the exercised shares, sufficient to cover the withholding obligation, and remits the proceeds to the employer. - **Cash payment from employee:** The employee provides a check or wire for the withholding amount. - **Same-day sale (cashless exercise):** The employee simultaneously exercises and sells all shares; the broker withholds and remits applicable taxes from the proceeds. For non-employee service providers (consultants, directors who are not employees), no payroll withholding is required, but the company must report the income on Form 1099-NEC. The recipient is responsible for estimated tax payments on the income. ## NSO exercise mechanics The holder exercises an NSO by delivering the exercise price to the company (or to the plan administrator acting as agent). Acceptable forms of payment typically include: - **Cash or check** - **Cashless exercise (broker-assisted same-day sale):** The broker advances the exercise price, the company issues shares, the broker sells enough shares to recover the advance and remit the exercise price to the company. - **Net exercise (net settlement):** The company delivers shares net of the shares needed to pay the exercise price, without requiring cash from the employee. The number of shares delivered equals (shares exercised × spread) / FMV. - **Stock-for-stock swap:** The holder delivers already-owned shares of company stock as payment; the company transfers a number of new shares equal in value to the spread. The plan document governs which payment methods are permissible. Administrators should confirm the method with the broker before processing. ## Post-termination exercise windows NSOs typically specify a post-termination exercise window - the period after separation during which vested options may be exercised. Common windows are 90 days for voluntary and involuntary termination (other than cause), 12 months for death or disability, and immediate cancellation for termination for cause. Unlike ISOs, there is no statutory limit on how long a post-termination window can be for NSOs. Some companies have adopted extended windows (five or ten years) for long-tenured employees. However, extending the window beyond the original 409A-compliant expiration date can constitute a modification that triggers 409A analysis. ## Section 409A and NSOs NSOs are generally exempt from Section 409A deferred compensation rules as long as the exercise price equals or exceeds FMV at grant and the option has no other deferral feature. If an NSO is granted with an exercise price below FMV - even inadvertently - it can become subject to 409A, which imposes an additional 20% excise tax plus interest on the option holder. This makes accurate 409A valuations critical for private-company grants. ## NSOs for non-employees NSOs granted to non-employee directors and consultants follow the same economic structure but differ in reporting and withholding. The grant may be taxable at grant if the option has a readily ascertainable FMV or the services are complete. For most grants to directors and advisors of private companies, taxation occurs at exercise. Income is reported on Form 1099-NEC (not W-2), and the recipient must pay self-employment tax. Companies often gross-up grants to non-employees to account for the self-employment tax burden, though this itself creates additional income.

title: RSUs & RSAs
summary: Restricted stock units (RSUs) are unfunded promises to deliver shares upon vesting, while restricted stock awards (RSAs) are actual share transfers subject to forfeiture conditions. RSUs are the dominant award type for public companies because they require no purchase price, no Section 409A complexity at grant, and trigger income only when shares are actually delivered.
text: ## RSUs versus RSAs: the core distinction The terms "restricted stock unit" and "restricted stock award" are frequently confused, but they describe fundamentally different instruments. A **restricted stock award (RSA)** is an actual transfer of shares at the time of grant. The shares are "restricted" because they are subject to a vesting schedule: unvested shares remain subject to forfeiture if the recipient leaves before satisfying the conditions. The recipient owns the shares immediately upon grant and has all shareholder rights - including voting and dividends - from day one, but those rights are contingent on remaining employed through the vesting period. A **restricted stock unit (RSU)** is not a share - it is a contractual promise to deliver shares (or cash) at a future date, contingent on the recipient remaining employed through the vesting period. Until vesting, the recipient is an unsecured creditor of the company and has no shareholder rights. The RSU converts into actual shares only when the vesting condition is satisfied and shares are delivered. ## Tax treatment at grant **RSAs:** Because RSAs involve an actual transfer of property, IRC § 83 applies immediately at grant. The excess of FMV over any purchase price paid is ordinary income in the year the property becomes substantially vested. If the stock is subject to a vesting schedule, the ordinary income is ordinarily recognized each year as installments vest. However, the recipient can elect under IRC § 83(b) to include the full excess of FMV over purchase price in income at grant rather than as the property vests. This election must be filed with the IRS within 30 days of the grant date - no extensions are permitted. If FMV at grant is very low (as with early-stage private company stock), an 83(b) election can lock in a low income inclusion and start the long-term capital gain clock running immediately. **RSUs:** RSUs are not taxable at grant because they are unfunded, unsecured promises. There is nothing of present value to tax. Under the economic benefit doctrine, taxation does not occur until the RSU delivers actual property with ascertainable value. ## Tax treatment at vesting and delivery For RSUs, the taxable event is delivery of shares - typically the date the vesting condition is satisfied and shares are transferred to the participant's brokerage account. At that moment, the FMV of the shares delivered is ordinary compensation income, subject to federal income tax withholding and FICA taxes. For RSAs (where no 83(b) was filed), each vesting tranche triggers ordinary income equal to the FMV of the shares on the vesting date, less any purchase price paid. The employer withholds taxes on each vesting event. ## Withholding mechanics for RSUs When RSU shares vest and are delivered, the employer must satisfy its withholding obligation. The predominant method for public company RSUs is: **Net share withholding (sell-to-cover):** On the vesting date, the plan administrator instructs the broker to withhold a number of shares equal in value to the tax withholding amount. The company reacquires those shares at FMV and uses the proceeds to pay the tax. The participant receives the remaining net shares in their brokerage account. Supplemental withholding rates apply to RSU income: 22% federal for amounts up to $1 million in the year and 37% for amounts over $1 million. State withholding varies by jurisdiction. Employees whose effective marginal rate exceeds the supplemental rate will owe additional tax at filing and should be advised to increase estimated tax payments or W-4 withholding. ## Double-trigger RSUs at private companies Private companies commonly grant RSUs with a double-trigger vesting structure. A double-trigger RSU requires two conditions to be satisfied before shares are delivered: (1) time-based vesting (the employee remains employed through the schedule), and (2) a liquidity event (the company completes an IPO, direct listing, or acquisition). This structure is used because RSU delivery at a private company would force employees to pay income tax on illiquid shares - shares they cannot sell to fund the tax. By adding a liquidity trigger, delivery is deferred until a market exists for the shares. Without the liquidity trigger, RSUs at private companies would violate Section 409A if structured as standard RSUs. The liquidity event is one of the permissible payment triggers under Section 409A, making the double-trigger structure compliant. When the company goes public, the previously unvested time-based tranche and the newly satisfied liquidity trigger both fire, and employees may face a large income recognition event as years of accumulated RSUs deliver simultaneously. ## RSA mechanics for early-stage companies RSAs are common at early-stage companies and for founder stock. The structure involves purchasing shares (often at par value or a low price reflecting early-stage FMV) subject to a vesting schedule that gives the company repurchase rights over unvested shares at the original purchase price. The 83(b) election is almost always advisable for founders receiving RSAs at a very low FMV, because it converts future appreciation from ordinary income into capital gain. The 30-day filing window is strict and is frequently missed by founders who do not have legal counsel at the moment of grant. Administrators should build a reminder into the grant workflow whenever RSAs are issued. ## Dividend equivalents on RSUs Because RSU holders are not shareholders, they do not receive actual dividends on unvested units. However, plan documents may provide for "dividend equivalents" - additional units or cash credits that accumulate based on dividends declared on the underlying shares. These credits are typically paid or settled at the same time as the underlying units vest. Dividend equivalents can constitute deferred compensation under Section 409A if not structured carefully.

title: Employee stock purchase plans (ESPPs)
summary: Employee stock purchase plans (ESPPs) allow employees to purchase company stock at a discount through payroll deductions. Qualified ESPPs under IRC Section 423 offer favorable tax treatment similar to ISOs, while non-qualified ESPPs do not require stockholder approval and offer more design flexibility. The discount, lookback period, and offering structure are the key design variables.
text: ## The ESPP structure An employee stock purchase plan (ESPP) is a company-sponsored program that allows eligible employees to purchase employer stock, typically at a discount, using accumulated payroll deductions. ESPPs operate on a cycle of offering periods - usually six or twelve months - during which employees contribute a percentage of their salary. At the end of each offering period, the accumulated funds are used to purchase shares at the designated purchase price. Congress established a favorable tax regime for ESPPs in IRC Section 423, modeled loosely on the ISO framework. Plans that comply with Section 423 are called "qualified" or "statutory" ESPPs and offer employees capital gains treatment on a portion of their gains. Plans that do not meet Section 423 requirements are "non-qualified" ESPPs, which function more like NSO grants: the discount at purchase is ordinary income, and there is no lookback feature unless the plan provides one. ## Section 423 qualified plan requirements To obtain the favorable tax treatment under IRC § 423, the plan must meet all of the following requirements: **Stockholder approval.** The plan must be approved by shareholders within twelve months before or after the board adopts it. **Equal rights and privileges.** All employees of the corporation (and participating subsidiaries) must be granted the same rights and privileges under the plan. However, the plan may exclude employees who have been employed less than two years, part-time or temporary employees, and employees who own 5% or more of the employer's stock. **Non-transferability.** Purchase rights may not be transferred other than by will or intestacy laws. **Maximum discount.** The purchase price may not be less than the lesser of 85% of FMV at the start of the offering period or 85% of FMV at the purchase date. **Maximum offering period.** No offering period may exceed 27 months (or 5 years if the price is set at a fixed formula based solely on offering-date FMV). **$25,000 accrual limit.** No employee may accrue the right to purchase more than $25,000 of stock annually. ## The lookback feature The most powerful feature of a well-designed Section 423 ESPP is the lookback. Under the 85%/85% rule, the purchase price is the lower of 85% of the offering-date stock price or 85% of the purchase-date stock price. This means that if the stock rises over the offering period, employees purchase at 85% of the lower offering-date price - capturing not just the discount but also the appreciation. Consider a 12-month offering period where stock starts at $20 and closes at $30. Employees purchase at $17 (85% of $20), representing an effective discount of $13 - or 43% - on the day-of-purchase price. If the stock instead falls to $15, employees purchase at $12.75 (85% of $15), capturing a 15% discount on current value. This asymmetric benefit - participants always buy at the lower price - is what makes ESPPs with lookbacks particularly valuable to employees. ## Tax treatment: qualifying dispositions For Section 423 plan shares, the tax treatment depends on whether the employee meets both statutory holding periods: - More than **two years** from the first day of the offering period (offering date), and - More than **one year** from the purchase date. If both tests are met: - The ordinary income component is the **lesser of** (a) the actual discount from offering-date FMV (i.e., FMV at offering date minus purchase price), or (b) the total gain (sale price minus purchase price). - All remaining gain is long-term capital gain. - The ordinary income is reported on Form W-2 in the year of sale, not the year of purchase. - The company reports the share transfer on Form 3922 in the year of purchase. ## Tax treatment: disqualifying dispositions A disqualifying disposition occurs when shares are sold before satisfying either holding period. In a disqualifying disposition: - The spread at purchase (FMV on purchase date minus purchase price) is ordinary income in the year of sale. - The employer must report this on Form W-2 and may be required to withhold, though some administrators handle ESPP disqualifying dispositions through supplemental payroll runs. - Any gain above the ordinary income component is capital gain (short-term or long-term depending on the holding period from purchase to sale). Disqualifying dispositions are common because employees often sell ESPP shares immediately to capture the guaranteed discount rather than holding for the qualifying period. ## Non-qualified ESPPs Non-qualified ESPPs are not subject to the Section 423 requirements and therefore have more design flexibility. They can provide different benefits to different employee groups, can be offered to contractors or non-employees, and need not receive stockholder approval. However, they offer no preferential tax treatment: the discount at purchase is ordinary income subject to payroll withholding, similar to an NSO exercise. ## Enrollment and contribution mechanics During open enrollment windows, eligible employees elect a contribution percentage (typically 1 - 15% of eligible pay, subject to plan limits). Contributions are deducted from each paycheck and accumulated in a notional account. At the end of the offering period (the purchase date), accumulated contributions are applied to purchase shares. Employees may typically withdraw contributions before the purchase date - common when stock prices fall significantly during the offering period. Most plans allow a single withdrawal per offering period; some allow unlimited changes. ## Form 3922 reporting For Section 423 ESPPs, the company must file Form 3922 with the IRS for each employee who first acquires stock under the plan during the calendar year. The form captures the offering date, purchase date, offering-date FMV, purchase-date FMV, purchase price paid, and number of shares transferred. This data is essential for employees to correctly calculate their gain and character in the year of sale.

title: Performance share units (PSUs)
summary: Performance share units are company shares you earn only if certain goals are met over a set period, such as revenue targets or stock-price performance against peers. Once earned and delivered, the shares are taxed as regular income based on their value that day.
text: ## What a PSU is A performance share unit is a promise to deliver company shares only if defined goals are achieved over a measurement window, usually three years. Unlike time-based restricted stock units, the payout is variable: plans commonly set a threshold, a target, and a maximum, so the final share count might range from nothing up to two or three times the target grant depending on how the company performs. PSUs are a favorite long-term incentive at public companies because they tie a large slice of executive pay directly to results shareholders care about. ## Performance goals Goals fall into two broad families. Operational or financial metrics - revenue growth, earnings per share, return on invested capital, cash flow - reward hitting internal business targets. Stock-based metrics, most often total shareholder return, reward how the stock does, frequently measured relative to a peer group or a market index rather than in absolute terms. Relative goals insulate participants somewhat from broad market swings, since they reward out-performance rather than a rising tide. ## Taxation For US tax purposes PSUs work much like RSUs. There is no tax at grant and none while units remain unearned. When the performance period ends, the earned shares are delivered and their fair value on the settlement date is ordinary compensation income, reported as wages and subject to income and employment tax withholding under IRC § 83 and § 3401. Your basis in the shares equals that taxed amount, and any later gain or loss when you sell is capital in nature. <Advanced> ## Professional detail ASC 718 draws a sharp line between performance conditions and market conditions, and the distinction drives both measurement and expense timing. A market condition - relative or absolute TSR is the classic example - is baked into grant-date fair value using a path-dependent valuation such as a Monte Carlo simulation. That value is fixed at grant and is never trued up: if the market goal is missed, the company still recognizes the full grant-date expense for awards whose service condition was satisfied. A performance condition (a revenue or EPS hurdle) is not valued into fair value; instead the company estimates the probable outcome and recognizes expense for the number of units expected to vest, adjusting cumulative expense as estimates change and reversing expense entirely if the goal is ultimately deemed not probable. Awards blending both condition types require careful bifurcation. Payout multipliers above target increase the units delivered and the corresponding expense accrual, while the per-unit grant-date fair value for the market-condition slice remains anchored to the simulation output. </Advanced>

title: SARs & phantom equity
summary: Stock appreciation rights pay you the increase in a share's value over time, and phantom stock tracks the value of shares without giving you real ones. Both can settle in cash or stock, and the payout is taxed as regular wage income when you receive it.
text: ## Stock appreciation rights A stock appreciation right entitles the holder to the increase in a share's value above a base price fixed at grant, measured over the life of the award. If the share value rises, the holder collects that spread; if it does not, the right expires worthless. Unlike an option, a SAR requires no cash outlay to exercise, which is why it is often described as a cashless form of upside participation. Settlement can be in cash or in an equivalent number of shares, and that choice drives the accounting. ## Phantom equity Phantom stock is a bookkeeping unit that mirrors the value of a real share without conveying ownership. Holders receive the economic benefit - appreciation, and sometimes dividend-equivalent credits - but have no voting rights and hold no actual stock. Private companies and partnerships use phantom plans to reward key people while keeping the real cap table closed. Payout is typically cash tied to share value at a defined event or date. ## Taxation For both instruments, the general rule is ordinary income at settlement, equal to the cash or share value received, reported as wages and subject to employment tax withholding. <Advanced> ## Professional detail The cash-versus-stock settlement decision has a major accounting consequence under ASC 718. A cash-settled SAR or phantom unit is classified as a liability: it is measured at fair value at grant and then remeasured at fair value every reporting period through settlement, so expense swings with the stock price and the final expense equals the actual cash paid. A stock-settled SAR that settles in a fixed share equivalent is generally equity-classified, measured once at grant-date fair value and not remeasured. Because these awards commonly pay out well after the right to the payment vests, they sit squarely within IRC § 409A. To avoid its punitive tax - immediate income inclusion plus a 20% additional tax and premium interest - a SAR must be granted at or above fair market value on stock of the service recipient with no additional deferral feature to qualify for the § 409A exemption, while phantom plans must specify permissible payment events and fixed times at the outset. Valuation of the underlying stock in private companies should be supportable, often via a § 409A appraisal. </Advanced>

title: Dividends & dividend equivalents
summary: Restricted stock can pay real dividends because you hold actual shares, while RSUs and options may instead pay dividend equivalents that mimic those payments. On unvested awards these amounts are usually treated as regular wage income rather than qualified dividends.
text: ## Dividends on restricted stock Because a holder of restricted stock owns actual shares from the grant date, the company can pay real dividends on that stock even while it remains subject to forfeiture. How those dividends are taxed depends on the award's status. If the shares are still unvested and no Section 83(b) election was made, the dividends are treated as additional compensation - ordinary wage income subject to withholding - rather than as dividend income. Once the stock vests, or if an 83(b) election was filed at grant, later dividends are taxed as ordinary dividends and can qualify for preferential qualified-dividend rates when the holding requirements are met. ## Dividend equivalents An RSU or option confers no ownership before settlement, so there is no share on which a dividend can be paid. To keep holders economically whole, plans may grant dividend equivalent rights that credit an amount matching what a real shareholder would have received. These can be paid in cash or as additional units, and on unvested awards they are compensation income taxed at ordinary rates, not qualified dividends. ## Structuring the timing The safest design ties dividend equivalents to the underlying award: they accrue and pay only if and when the award vests and settles. <Advanced> ## Professional detail The central compliance risk with dividend equivalents is IRC § 409A. When equivalents are granted in connection with unvested RSUs or performance units, they should be structured so that payment occurs on the same schedule as the underlying award rather than on the company's ordinary dividend payment dates. Treasury guidance treats a dividend equivalent that is paid at the same time as the underlying stock right as not creating a separate deferral of compensation, whereas an equivalent payable on an independent schedule can constitute its own nonqualified deferred compensation arrangement subject to § 409A's timing rules - with the 20% additional tax and premium interest as the penalty for a defect. For performance-based awards it is common to accrue equivalents on target units and true them up to the shares actually earned, forfeiting equivalents on units that never vest. Under ASC 718, dividends and dividend equivalents paid on awards that ultimately vest are charged to retained earnings, while amounts attributable to awards that are forfeited are reclassified as additional compensation cost. The § 83(b) election remains pivotal for restricted stock, converting post-election distributions from wages into dividend income eligible, when holding-period conditions are satisfied, for the lower rates of IRC § 1(h)(11). </Advanced>

title: Grant & acceptance
summary: An equity award becomes real when the board or its delegated committee approves it and the recipient has a mutual understanding of the key terms. Signing or clicking to accept the grant agreement often locks in consent to restrictive covenants and clawback provisions, so acceptance is more than a formality.
text: ## How a grant comes into existence Equity awards start with corporate authority. A company's equity plan is approved by the board and, for public companies, by shareholders. The board typically delegates authority to grant individual awards to a compensation committee, and many plans permit further delegation to officers for non-executive grants within set limits. An award is only valid once it clears whatever approval process the plan and corporate law require. Approval alone does not fix the accounting grant date. Under ASC 718 the grant date arrives when four conditions align: the award has been approved, the employer and recipient share a mutual understanding of the key terms, the employer is obligated to deliver the award once service or performance conditions are met, and the recipient begins to benefit from, or be affected by, changes in the underlying share value. This grant date is the measurement date on which the award's fair value is calculated. ## Why acceptance matters The grant agreement is the contract between company and recipient. It incorporates the plan document and layers on award-specific terms: vesting schedule, number of shares, exercise price for options, expiration, and treatment on termination or a corporate transaction. Most companies now handle acceptance electronically through an equity platform, where the recipient reviews and clicks to accept. Acceptance is significant because it frequently records consent to obligations that run in the company's favor. These can include clawback or recoupment rights, non-competition and non-solicitation covenants, and confidentiality terms. By accepting, the recipient generally agrees to be bound by those provisions in exchange for the award. Some plans provide that an unaccepted award is forfeited after a deadline, and vesting, exercise, or settlement may be blocked until acceptance is recorded. <Advanced> ## Professional detail For accounting purposes, a "mutual understanding of key terms" can be presumed at approval when the award's terms are fixed and communicated, but awards with terms subject to later determination (for example, performance targets not yet set) may have a later service-inception or grant date. A service-inception date preceding the grant date requires accruing expense before grant-date fair value is known, based on a fair value estimate. For stock options and stock appreciation rights, §409A requires the exercise price to be at least the fair market value of the underlying stock on the grant date; private companies typically rely on an independent §409A valuation. Setting the price below fair market value creates deferred compensation subject to §409A penalties. ISOs must additionally satisfy IRC §422, including a price at or above fair market value and, for 10% owners, at least 110%. </Advanced>

title: Vesting
summary: Vesting is the process by which an equity award recipient earns irrevocable ownership of shares or options over time, typically conditioned on continued employment. Understanding vesting schedules, cliff periods, acceleration provisions, and the distinction between time-based and performance-based vesting is essential for both plan administrators and participants.
text: ## The purpose of vesting Vesting schedules serve several functions simultaneously. For the company, vesting creates retention incentives - employees who leave before their shares vest forfeit unvested equity. For tax purposes, vesting (or the lifting of a substantial risk of forfeiture) determines when many equity awards become taxable under IRC § 83. For accounting, the vesting period generally defines the requisite service period over which compensation cost is recognized under ASC 718. ## Time-based vesting schedules The dominant vesting structure for US equity grants is a four-year schedule with a one-year cliff. Under this structure: - Nothing vests for the first 12 months of service. - On the first anniversary of the grant (or start date, depending on the plan), 25% of the award vests at once - this is the "cliff." - The remaining 75% vests ratably over the following three years, typically in monthly or quarterly increments. Variations are common. Early-stage startups may use three-year or two-year schedules. Public companies sometimes use annual vesting for refresher grants (25% per year with no cliff). Some companies use back-weighted schedules where fewer shares vest in early years and more in later years, to strengthen long-term retention. ### Vesting commencement dates The vesting schedule ordinarily begins on one of three dates: - **Grant date:** Most common. Vesting begins on the date the board approves the award. - **Start date (or anniversary date):** Vesting begins on the employee's hire date or most recent service anniversary, regardless of the grant date. - **Vesting commencement date:** A specific date specified in the award agreement, sometimes set before the grant date to credit prior service. Administrators should note that the grant date and vesting commencement date can be different, and the plan document should specify which triggers the cliff and each subsequent vesting date. ## Performance-based vesting Performance share units (PSUs) and many restricted stock awards vest based on achievement of performance metrics rather than (or in addition to) time. Common performance metrics include: - **Relative total shareholder return (rTSR):** Performance measured against a peer group or index. If the company's stock outperforms 75% of the peer group, employees might receive 150% of the target award. - **Revenue or EPS growth:** Absolute or relative financial targets over a 1 - 3 year performance period. - **Operational metrics:** Customer growth, product milestones, or other non-financial targets. Performance awards typically have a target number of shares (100%) and a payout range (0% - 200%, for example). The actual number of shares that vest depends on measured performance against the target at the end of the performance period. ### Certification and settlement Vesting of performance awards does not occur automatically at period end. The Compensation Committee or board must formally certify achievement of the performance metrics and determine the payout multiplier. This certification step is legally required to establish when the forfeiture restriction lapses and the award vests for tax and accounting purposes. ## Acceleration provisions Award agreements frequently include provisions that accelerate vesting under specified circumstances: ### Single-trigger acceleration All unvested equity vests upon a change in control, regardless of what happens to the employee. Single-trigger is rare in current practice because acquiring companies typically want unvested equity to retain employees post-deal. ### Double-trigger acceleration The most common structure: a portion of unvested equity accelerates only if a change in control occurs AND the employee is involuntarily terminated (or resigns for "good reason") within a specified post-close period, often 12 - 24 months. This protects employees from losing unvested equity due to a deal while preserving the acquirer's ability to use equity as a retention tool. ### Disability and death acceleration Plans commonly accelerate vesting - partially or fully - upon the death or permanent disability of the participant. The definition of "disability" in the plan document controls; administrators should reference it precisely rather than relying on informal characterizations. ## Tracking vesting and maintaining accurate records For each grant, the plan administration system must record: - Award type, grant date, vesting commencement date - Full vesting schedule (cliff date, monthly/quarterly increment amounts, full vest date) - Any acceleration provisions applicable to the grant - Termination date, if applicable, and the resulting accelerated or forfeited tranche split Errors in vesting records can lead to tax withholding mistakes (vesting at wrong amounts on wrong dates), incorrect ASC 718 expense recognition, and disputes with employees who believe they vested more than they did. Periodic reconciliation of the plan administration system against the ledger is a critical control. ## Early exercise and 83(b) elections Some option plans allow "early exercise" - exercising unvested stock options before they vest. Early-exercised shares are typically restricted: the company holds a repurchase right over unvested shares at the original exercise price, which lapses as the underlying vesting schedule is satisfied. Early exercise combined with an IRC § 83(b) election allows option holders (most commonly founders) to start the long-term capital gains clock at the time of exercise. The 83(b) election must be filed with the IRS within 30 days of the exercise date. The income recognized at the 83(b) election is the spread at exercise - which for early-exercise of options shortly after grant is often zero or very small if the exercise price equals FMV.

title: Exercise
summary: Exercising a stock option converts the right to buy shares into actual share ownership by paying the exercise price. The method of exercise (cash, cashless, net exercise) determines the participant's out-of-pocket cost, share count, and tax withholding mechanics. For ISOs, the decision of when to exercise has significant AMT and capital gains implications.
text: ## What exercise means Exercising a stock option is the act of electing to purchase the underlying shares at the exercise price specified in the option agreement. Until exercise, the option holder has only a right - not an obligation - to buy shares. Exercise converts that right into actual share ownership. Once shares are purchased, the option is extinguished and the holder becomes a stockholder (subject to whatever restrictions apply to the shares). Exercise is only available for vested options. Unvested options cannot be exercised unless the plan provides for early exercise, which is a separate feature and subject to its own restrictions. ## Exercise methods ### Cash exercise The option holder sends a check or wire for the full exercise price to the company or its transfer agent, and the company issues shares in return. This method requires the participant to have sufficient liquid funds and results in the participant owning shares with no immediate proceeds. **When it makes sense:** When the participant wants to hold shares for long-term gain, has liquidity available, and the exercise price is low relative to the amount they can afford. ### Cashless exercise (same-day sale) The participant authorizes a broker to advance the exercise price, the company issues shares, the broker immediately sells all shares in the open market, and the proceeds are used to repay the broker and cover withholding taxes. The participant receives net cash proceeds. **When it makes sense:** When the participant needs liquidity, does not want to hold shares, or does not have funds for a cash exercise. **ISO caution:** A same-day sale of ISO shares in the year of exercise constitutes a disqualifying disposition, eliminating ISO tax benefits. Participants exercising ISOs who want qualifying-disposition treatment must hold shares past year-end. ### Sell-to-cover The participant exercises and simultaneously sells only enough shares to cover the exercise price and withholding taxes. The remaining shares are held in the participant's brokerage account. This is a hybrid approach. ### Net exercise (net settlement) Instead of paying the exercise price in cash, the company delivers a net number of shares equal to the option's intrinsic value. The formula is: **Net shares = (Market Price − Exercise Price) × Shares Exercised / Market Price**. No cash changes hands; the participant simply receives fewer shares. Net exercise is often used for private company exercises or for convenience in public company plans. ### Stock swap The participant delivers already-owned shares of company stock as payment for the exercise price. The value of the surrendered shares must equal the exercise price. The surrendered shares must typically have been held long enough to avoid a disqualifying disposition if they are ISO shares. ## Timing considerations for ISOs The ISO exercise timing decision is more complex than for NSOs because: 1. **AMT exposure:** Exercising ISOs and holding shares creates an AMT preference item. If the spread is large, the resulting AMT can be significant. 2. **Qualifying disposition clock:** The two-year grant/one-year exercise holding periods begin running upon exercise. Exercising early - when the spread is small - means the employee reaches qualifying-disposition status sooner and with lower ordinary income exposure. 3. **Same-year sale rule:** Exercising and selling ISO shares in the same calendar year eliminates the AMT preference but is a disqualifying disposition. This may actually produce a better after-tax result than holding if the employee's regular tax rate is lower than their AMT rate. 4. **Section 422(d) limit:** No more than $100,000 of options (by grant-date FMV) can first become exercisable in any year under ISO treatment. This doesn't limit when options can be exercised, but it affects which tranches qualify as ISOs versus NSOs. ## Post-termination exercise windows After a participant terminates employment, vested options can generally be exercised during a specified post-termination exercise period (PTEP). Key rules: - **ISOs:** Must be exercised within 3 months of termination to retain ISO status (12 months for disability; no statutory window for death, though the plan may specify one). Options not exercised within 3 months automatically convert to NSOs for tax purposes. - **NSOs:** No statutory time limit, but the plan document specifies the window - commonly 90 days for voluntary or involuntary termination (other than cause) and immediate cancellation for termination for cause. Administrators must notify departing employees of their PTEP and the date by which options must be exercised. The termination date used to start the PTEP should be the last day of employment, not the date any notice is given. ## Blackout periods and trading restrictions Public company employees may be restricted from exercising options during blackout periods - typically the period around quarterly earnings announcements. Additionally, Section 16 officers cannot sell shares acquired upon exercise within six months of a prior offsetting transaction under Section 16(b). These restrictions can prevent exercise even when options are about to expire. Administrators should maintain a blackout calendar and communicate it clearly to option holders. Participants with options nearing expiration during a blackout may need alternative arrangements (such as a pre-established 10b5-1 plan) to ensure they can exercise before expiration. ## Processing an exercise: administrator checklist 1. Verify the option is vested and within its exercise window. 2. Confirm the participant is not subject to a blackout or trading restriction. 3. Collect the exercise price using the elected payment method. 4. Calculate withholding for NSOs: spread × applicable withholding rates. 5. Issue shares to the participant's designated brokerage account or record in the cap table. 6. For ISOs: no withholding at exercise, but document the FMV and spread for Form 3921. 7. Update the plan administration system and option ledger. 8. File Form 3921 (ISOs) or process Form W-2 supplemental payroll (NSOs) on the appropriate schedule.

title: Settlement & release
summary: Settlement is the moment shares (or their cash value) are actually delivered to the recipient, usually when restricted stock units vest. Because vesting of RSUs is a taxable event, companies withhold taxes at that point, most often by holding back or selling some of the shares.
text: ## From vesting to shares in hand A restricted stock unit is a promise to deliver shares (or cash) once conditions are met; it is not stock until it settles. Settlement is the delivery event. For most RSU programs, settlement occurs at vesting or within a short window afterward, and the recipient receives actual shares that can be held or sold. Under IRC §83, the value of property transferred for services is included in income when it is no longer subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture. For a typical time-vesting RSU, that is the vest date, and the amount included is the fair market value of the shares on that date. Because this is wage income, the employer must withhold federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare, and the value is reported on Form W-2. The employee's basis in the delivered shares equals the amount already taxed, so later gain or loss is measured from the vest-date value. ## Covering the tax bill Employers use a few mechanisms to satisfy withholding at settlement. Net share settlement (also called share withholding) reduces the shares delivered: the company keeps back enough shares to equal the tax obligation and cancels them, remitting cash to the tax authorities. Sell-to-cover delivers the full share count to a broker, which immediately sells a portion on the open market to raise the withholding cash. A cash payment option lets the recipient fund taxes separately and keep all shares. The choice affects share count, dilution, and cash flow. Net settlement conserves the company's cash but uses treasury or authorized shares; sell-to-cover puts shares into the market but keeps cash outlay off the company. Withholding is generally required at supplemental wage rates for the federal income component. <Advanced> ## Professional detail RSUs are deferred compensation, so their settlement timing is governed by §409A unless an exemption applies. The short-term deferral rule in Treas. Reg. §1.409A-1(b)(4) exempts amounts paid by the 15th day of the third month after the end of the year in which the substantial risk of forfeiture lapses (the employer's or employee's taxable year, whichever is later). Settling within that window generally keeps the award outside §409A's restrictions. If settlement is deliberately delayed beyond the short-term deferral period, the arrangement must comply with §409A: the payment event and timing must be fixed at grant, and elections to defer further must meet the timing and subsequent-deferral rules. Non-compliance triggers immediate income inclusion plus a 20% additional tax and premium-interest penalties on the employee. </Advanced>

title: Liquidity & exits
summary: Liquidity events - IPOs, tender offers, secondary sales, and mergers or acquisitions - are when equity can finally be turned into cash. How each award is treated depends on the deal terms and the plan, ranging from assumption and substitution to cash-out or acceleration, and each path has its own tax timing.
text: ## The paths to liquidity Private-company equity has value on paper long before it can be sold. Liquidity events convert it to cash. An initial public offering registers shares for public trading; a tender offer or company-sponsored buyback lets holders sell a defined number of shares to a buyer or the company; and secondary sales allow private transfers to investors, often subject to company transfer restrictions and rights of first refusal. Each event may have eligibility rules, pricing, and windows set by the company or the deal. ## Equity in mergers and acquisitions An acquisition forces a decision about outstanding awards, and the merger agreement and equity plan dictate the outcome. Common treatments include assumption, where the acquirer takes over existing awards on their current terms; substitution, where awards are replaced with economically equivalent awards over the acquirer's stock; cash-out, where vested awards (and sometimes unvested ones, paid over the original schedule) are exchanged for cash equal to deal value less any exercise price; cancellation of awards that are underwater or unvested without replacement; and acceleration, where vesting is advanced in whole or part. Acceleration is often structured as single-trigger (vesting on the change in control itself) or double-trigger (vesting only if the deal is followed by a qualifying termination). Double-trigger is common for broad-based awards because it retains talent through the transition. ## Tax timing on liquidity Selling shares is a capital transaction: gain or loss is measured against basis, with long-term rates available if the holding period exceeds one year. Cashing out a vested option or SAR generally produces ordinary compensation income equal to the spread, subject to withholding. Accelerated RSUs settled in the deal produce ordinary income at settlement. A lock-up delays the ability to sell but does not by itself delay the tax already triggered by vesting or settlement. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Cash-out and acceleration provisions must respect §409A. Substituting or accelerating deferred-compensation awards on a change in control is permitted only if the transaction meets the §409A definition of a change in control event, or if payment timing otherwise complies; a poorly drafted cash-out can accelerate a §409A payment impermissibly and trigger the 20% additional tax. Large change-in-control payments can also implicate the golden parachute rules of IRC §280G and §4999, which deny the company a deduction and impose a 20% excise tax on "excess parachute payments" to disqualified individuals when total change-in-control compensation reaches three times the individual's base amount. Post-IPO resales by affiliates remain subject to SEC Rule 144, including holding-period, volume, and Form 144 requirements, in addition to any contractual lock-up. </Advanced>

title: Option taxation (ISO/NSO, AMT)
summary: Stock options are taxed differently depending on whether they are ISOs or NSOs. NSOs generate ordinary income and payroll taxes at exercise, with any post-exercise gain taxed as capital gain. ISOs generate no ordinary income at exercise for regular tax purposes, but the exercise spread is an AMT preference item that can create significant alternative minimum tax liability.
text: ## The two option types and their tax frameworks Stock options granted in employment contexts are either incentive stock options (ISOs), governed by IRC § 422, or non-qualified stock options (NSOs), governed by the general principles of IRC § 83. The fundamental distinction is when and how the option spread is taxed: - **NSOs:** Spread is ordinary income at exercise. Subject to income tax, Social Security, and Medicare. Company gets a deduction. Straightforward. - **ISOs:** No ordinary income at exercise (for regular tax purposes). Instead, the spread is an AMT preference item. If you hold qualifying-disposition requirements, the entire gain from exercise price to sale price is long-term capital gain. ## NSO taxation in detail ### At grant No taxable event. NSOs without a readily ascertainable FMV (the vast majority) are not taxable when granted. ### At exercise The spread - FMV on the exercise date minus the exercise price - is ordinary compensation income. If the spread is $50 per share and you exercise 1,000 shares, you have $50,000 of ordinary income. This appears on your W-2 and is subject to: - Federal income tax at your marginal rate (up to 37% in 2024 - 2025) - Social Security tax at 6.2% on wages up to the Social Security wage base ($168,600 in 2024) - Medicare at 1.45% (plus an additional 0.9% if total wages exceed $200,000 for single filers, or $250,000 for married filing jointly) Your employer must withhold supplemental income tax (22% flat for most employees; 37% for wages above $1 million in the year). ### After exercise Your cost basis in the shares is the FMV on the exercise date. Gain or loss from that basis to the eventual sale price is capital gain or loss. Holding the shares for more than 12 months from exercise generates long-term capital gain; selling within 12 months is short-term gain at ordinary rates. ## ISO taxation in detail ### At grant No taxable event. Same as NSOs. ### At exercise - regular tax Under IRC § 422, no ordinary income is recognized when an ISO is exercised. The option holder receives shares without any W-2 income. The employer does not withhold FICA or income tax. ### At exercise - AMT Under IRC § 56(b)(3), the ISO spread is an adjustment to alternative minimum taxable income. The spread increases your AMTI, and the AMT is calculated on AMTI after the AMT exemption. For 2024, the AMT exemption is $85,700 for single filers and $133,300 for married filing jointly, phasing out at higher AMTI levels. If your tentative minimum tax (AMTI × 26% up to $220,700; 28% above) exceeds your regular tax, you owe the difference as AMT. Large ISO spreads in high-valuation years can generate substantial AMT bills even before the employee has sold any shares - creating a situation where taxes are owed on paper gains. ### Qualifying disposition If you hold ISO shares for more than two years from the grant date AND more than one year from the exercise date, any sale is a qualifying disposition. The entire gain from exercise price to sale price is long-term capital gain. There is no ordinary income. The employer does not report a W-2 inclusion (although Form 3921 must still be filed). ### Disqualifying disposition If you sell ISO shares before meeting both holding periods, the ordinary income component equals the lesser of: - The spread at exercise (FMV at exercise minus exercise price), or - The actual gain realized (sale price minus exercise price) This ordinary income is reported on your W-2 in the year of sale (not the year of exercise), and all remaining gain is capital gain. ## The AMT credit AMT paid because of ISO adjustments - not because of other AMT preference items - generates a minimum tax credit (MTC) under IRC § 53. The credit carryforward reduces regular tax in future years when regular tax exceeds the tentative minimum tax. **Example:** An employee pays $20,000 of AMT in Year 1 due to an ISO exercise. In Year 2, her regular tax liability is $35,000 and her tentative minimum tax is $10,000. She can apply $25,000 of MTC (the excess of regular over tentative minimum tax) to reduce her Year 2 regular tax from $35,000 to $10,000. The remaining MTC carries to Year 3 and beyond. ## Planning strategies for ISO exercises **Exercise early in the year.** If you plan to hold for a qualifying disposition, exercising in January gives you the full year to decide whether to sell before December 31 without creating a disqualifying disposition in the exercise year. **Model AMT before exercising.** Use the current year's AMT exemption and phaseout thresholds to estimate whether an exercise will trigger AMT. Factors include your W-2 income, deductions, and the size of the ISO spread. **Consider a partial same-year sale.** If the AMT bill would be unmanageable, selling some ISO shares before December 31 of the exercise year creates a disqualifying disposition on those shares (eliminating their AMT preference) while preserving the qualifying-disposition path for the remaining shares. **Track cost basis for both regular tax and AMT.** For AMT purposes, the cost basis of ISO shares is the FMV at exercise (not the exercise price), because the spread was already included in AMTI. Keeping two sets of records avoids double-taxation when the shares are eventually sold.

title: RSU & ESPP tax
summary: RSUs create ordinary income at vesting equal to the FMV of shares delivered, subject to income tax withholding and FICA. ESPPs create a more complex tax picture: qualifying dispositions split gain between ordinary income and capital gain, while disqualifying dispositions convert the purchase discount to ordinary income. Administrators must understand both to process withholding correctly and generate accurate W-2 and 1099 reporting.
text: ## RSU taxation: timing and mechanics Restricted stock units generate ordinary income when shares are delivered to the participant - in most cases, the vesting date. At the moment of delivery, the full fair market value of shares delivered is compensation income under IRC § 83(a), included in gross income in the year of delivery. ### The vesting taxable event When RSU shares vest, the administrator must: 1. Determine the FMV of the shares on the vesting date (closing market price for public company shares). 2. Calculate the withholding obligation: FMV × number of shares vesting × applicable withholding rates. 3. Execute the chosen withholding method (typically net share withholding). 4. Report the income through payroll. The income recognized equals the number of shares vesting multiplied by the FMV on the vesting date. This amount is subject to: - **Federal income tax withholding:** 22% supplemental rate on amounts up to $1 million in the year; 37% above. - **Social Security tax:** 6.2% on wages up to the annual wage base. - **Medicare tax:** 1.45% on all wages, plus 0.9% additional Medicare tax on wages exceeding $200,000 for single filers. - **State income tax:** Varies by state. Multi-state employees may owe tax in multiple states based on where they worked during the vesting period. ### W-2 reporting RSU income is included in Box 1 (Total Wages) and Box 3 and Box 5 (Social Security and Medicare wages) of Form W-2. The value of RSUs (gross income before tax withholding) must also be reported in Box 12 with Code V (for restricted stock, the gross income from RSU delivery). ## Net share withholding in practice Net share withholding is the dominant RSU withholding method for public companies. Here is how the transaction flows: 1. On the vesting date, the plan administration system identifies the vesting grant and calculates the tax withholding amount. 2. The administrator instructs the custodian broker to withhold X shares (where X = withholding amount / FMV per share, rounded up). 3. The broker reacquires those shares at the current market price. 4. The broker remits the proceeds to the employer (or to the IRS via the employer's payroll tax account). 5. The remaining shares are delivered to the participant's brokerage account. The participant receives a net share quantity. From the participant's perspective, they see shares appear in their account on vest date, with a cost basis equal to the FMV on that date (because the ordinary income has already been recognized on that day). ## Post-vesting capital gain After shares are delivered at vesting, the participant's basis is the FMV on the delivery date. Any appreciation or depreciation from that point is capital gain or loss: - If held more than 12 months from delivery, long-term capital gain rates apply (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income). - If sold within 12 months, short-term gain at ordinary income rates. - If shares decline in value after vesting, the participant has a capital loss - but cannot recover the income taxes already paid on the vesting-date FMV. ## ESPP taxation: qualifying versus disqualifying dispositions ESPP tax treatment splits into two regimes depending on whether the participant meets both statutory holding periods: - More than **2 years** from the first day of the offering period (the "offering date"), AND - More than **1 year** from the purchase date. ### Qualifying disposition When both holding periods are satisfied, the tax treatment is favorable: **Ordinary income:** The lesser of: (a) The actual discount from the offering-date price: (Offering-date FMV − Purchase price) × shares sold, or (b) Total gain realized: (Sale price − Purchase price) × shares sold. **Long-term capital gain:** Any remaining gain above the ordinary income component. **Example:** Offering date FMV $20, purchase price $17 (85% × $20), sale price $35 two years later. - Ordinary income = lesser of ($20 − $17) × shares or ($35 − $17) × shares = $3/share ordinary income. - Long-term capital gain = ($35 − $20) × shares = $15/share. - W-2 reporting in the year of sale. ### Disqualifying disposition When shares are sold before satisfying either holding period (typically an immediate-sale after purchase): **Ordinary income:** The spread at purchase = (FMV on purchase date − Purchase price) × shares sold. This is regardless of whether the shares are sold at a loss afterward. **Capital gain or loss:** Sale price minus FMV on purchase date. Short-term if held less than 12 months from purchase; long-term if held more than 12 months. **Example:** Offering date FMV $20, purchase date FMV $28, purchase price $17 (85% × $20), same-day sale at $28. - Ordinary income = ($28 − $17) × shares = $11/share. - Capital gain = $0 (sold at purchase-date FMV). ### W-2 and withholding for ESPP Unlike RSU vesting, ESPP purchases themselves do not trigger withholding - participants purchase shares using after-tax payroll deductions. The withholding obligation arises only when a disqualifying disposition is reported: - If a disqualifying disposition occurs, the ordinary income element must be reported on the participant's W-2. Some administrators handle this through a supplemental payroll run in the year the disqualifying disposition is reported. - Qualifying disposition ordinary income is also reported on W-2 in the year of sale but typically without withholding. The Form 3922 (filed by the company in the year of purchase) provides participants with the data needed to correctly compute their tax at the time of sale: offering date, purchase date, offering-date FMV, purchase-date FMV, and purchase price.

title: Capital gains, holding periods & 83(b)
summary: Capital gains on equity compensation are taxed at preferential rates if shares are held long enough - more than 12 months generally qualifies for long-term rates, but ISO qualifying dispositions add a second 2-year holding period from grant. The Section 83(b) election allows recipients of restricted property to elect immediate ordinary income recognition in exchange for starting the long-term capital gains clock at grant.
text: ## Capital gains: the basic framework Capital gains on equity compensation arise when an employee sells shares for more than their cost basis. The federal tax rates depend on how long the taxpayer held the shares: **Short-term capital gain:** Shares held for 12 months or less from the date of acquisition. Taxed at the taxpayer's ordinary income rates (up to 37% in 2024). **Long-term capital gain:** Shares held for more than 12 months. Taxed at preferential rates: - 0% for taxable income up to approximately $47,025 (single) / $94,050 (MFJ) in 2024. - 15% for most taxpayers above those thresholds. - 20% for high-income taxpayers (income above approximately $518,900 single / $583,750 MFJ in 2024). - The 3.8% net investment income tax (NIIT) under IRC § 1411 applies to capital gains of taxpayers with modified adjusted gross income above $200,000 (single) / $250,000 (MFJ), effectively raising the top rate to 23.8%. ## Holding period rules by award type **NSO shares:** The holding period begins on the exercise date. Shares sold within 12 months of exercise generate short-term capital gain; after 12 months, long-term. **ISO shares - qualifying disposition:** The holding period begins on the exercise date for the one-year test, but the grant date also applies for the two-year test. Both must be satisfied. If both are met, the entire gain (sale price minus exercise price) is long-term capital gain. **ISO shares - disqualifying disposition:** The holding period for the capital gain component begins on the exercise date. The ordinary income component (lesser of spread at exercise or total gain) is not subject to capital gains rates. **RSU shares:** The holding period begins on the delivery date (the date the shares are released into the participant's account at vesting). There is no connection to the grant date. **RSA shares (no 83(b) election):** The holding period begins on the vesting date for each tranche. The cost basis for each tranche is the FMV on the date that tranche vested. **RSA shares (83(b) election filed):** The holding period begins on the transfer date (grant date). The cost basis is the amount of income recognized under the 83(b) election, plus any purchase price paid. ## The Section 83(b) election Under IRC § 83(b), a recipient of property subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture may elect to include the value of that property in income immediately at the time of transfer, rather than waiting until the property vests. Filing this election converts future appreciation from ordinary income into capital gain and starts the long-term holding period clock at the transfer date. ### What the election covers The 83(b) election is available for restricted property - most commonly: - Restricted stock awards (RSAs) purchased at or below FMV - Shares acquired through early exercise of stock options (before vesting) - Founders' stock subject to repurchase rights The election is **not** available for RSUs, because RSUs are not transfers of property - they are unfunded promises. The underlying property (shares) is not transferred until vesting, at which point the 83(b) window has not yet begun. ### How to file Under Treasury Regulation § 1.83-2 and the safe harbor in Rev. Proc. 2012-29, the election must include: - The name, address, and taxpayer identification number of the taxpayer - A description of the property transferred - The date of transfer and the taxable year for which the election is made - The nature of any restrictions on the property - The FMV of the property at the time of transfer, determined without regard to restrictions other than those that will never lapse - The amount paid for the property - A statement that copies have been provided to the employer The election must be filed with the IRS service center where the taxpayer files their return, postmarked or submitted no later than 30 days after the transfer date. A copy must be attached to the taxpayer's return for the year of transfer. A copy must also be provided to the employer. ### Tax consequences If an 83(b) election is filed: - The excess of FMV over purchase price is ordinary income in the year of transfer. - The holding period begins on the transfer date. - All future appreciation is capital gain (short-term or long-term depending on how long shares are held from transfer). - If the property is subsequently forfeited (e.g., the employee leaves before vesting), the forfeiture loss is a capital loss limited to the purchase price - the ordinary income recognized at the time of election is not recoverable. ### When the election makes sense The 83(b) election is most valuable when: 1. The FMV at grant equals or closely approximates the purchase price, so the ordinary income recognized at election is minimal (ideally zero). 2. The stock is expected to appreciate significantly over the vesting period. 3. The recipient will hold shares long enough to qualify for long-term capital gain treatment from the grant date. For a founder receiving shares at par value ($0.0001 per share) at incorporation, an 83(b) election generates zero ordinary income and starts the long-term capital gain clock immediately. Years later, when the company is worth significantly more, all appreciation from the founding date is long-term capital gain. ### When the election does NOT make sense - When FMV significantly exceeds the purchase price and would generate a large immediate tax bill. - When the stock is unlikely to appreciate (or may decline). - When the recipient cannot hold the stock long enough to benefit from long-term rates. - For RSU holders, who are ineligible to file the election.

title: Payroll & withholding mechanics
summary: When equity compensation becomes taxable, it is treated as wages and runs through payroll. Employers withhold federal income tax at supplemental rates, apply Social Security and Medicare taxes, and must deposit those amounts to the IRS on strict deadlines.
text: ## Equity income is wages When equity compensation becomes taxable - RSUs at vest, NSOs at exercise, a disqualifying ESPP or ISO disposition - the resulting spread is compensation and flows through payroll like any paycheck. The employer reports it on Form W-2 and must withhold federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare. ## Supplemental wage withholding Equity income is a "supplemental wage" (pay other than regular salary). Under IRS rules, employers most commonly withhold federal income tax at a flat rate: 22% on supplemental wages up to $1,000,000 in a calendar year, and a mandatory 37% on the portion above $1,000,000. Because 22% may sit below an employee's actual marginal rate, high earners frequently find that withholding falls short of what they owe, so estimated payments or extra withholding may be needed to avoid an underpayment. ## FICA taxes and timing Separately, FICA applies. Social Security tax is withheld on wages up to the annual wage base; Medicare has no cap. An additional 0.9% Medicare tax applies to wages over statutory thresholds ($200,000 for a single filer at the employer-withholding level). For RSUs, FICA is generally due when the award vests and is no longer subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture - this can occur even though the employee has not sold any shares and has received no cash. ## Funding the withholding Because vesting produces a tax bill without cash, companies use mechanisms to fund it. Sell-to-cover automatically sells a portion of the newly vested shares on the open market and remits the proceeds. Net settlement (share withholding) instead has the company withhold shares with a value equal to the required tax and deliver only the net shares, avoiding a market transaction. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Deposit timing is governed by IRS rules and can be aggressive for large equity events. Employers are either monthly or semiweekly depositors based on their lookback-period liability, but the next-day deposit rule requires that once accumulated undeposited employment taxes reach $100,000, the deposit is due by the next business day. A single large vest or coordinated exercise can trigger this $100,000 threshold on its own, forcing an expedited deposit regardless of the employer's normal schedule. Late deposits expose the employer to graduated failure-to-deposit penalties, so payroll and equity teams typically coordinate closely around known vesting dates and secondary-liquidity events. </Advanced>

title: Multistate & mobility
summary: Equity income earned by employees who work in more than one state must be split among those states, usually by tracking workdays over the period from grant to vesting. States credit residents for tax paid elsewhere, but employees who move can still owe tax to a former state on income tied to work performed there.
text: ## Why mobility complicates equity tax Equity compensation is earned over time - typically the period between grant and vesting or exercise. When an employee lives or works in more than one state during that window, states each assert a claim to the portion of the income attributable to work performed within their borders. This turns a single vesting event into a multi-state sourcing exercise. ## Workday allocation The dominant method is workday allocation. A state taxes the fraction of the equity income equal to the days worked in that state during the service period divided by total workdays in the period. For RSUs, the period is generally grant to vest; for stock options, many states use grant to exercise. Because states do not adopt identical periods or day-counting conventions, the sums can overlap, and careful records of where an employee physically worked are essential. ## Residency and credits An employee's state of residence generally taxes all of their income, including equity income sourced elsewhere. To prevent double taxation, resident states offer a credit for income tax paid to other states on the same income. The credit is capped at the resident state's own tax on that income, so if the source state's rate is higher, some tax may not be fully recovered. ## Trailing liabilities after relocation Relocating does not erase a prior state's claim. If an award was partly earned by work performed in a former state, that state can tax the corresponding slice of income when the award later vests or is exercised - a "trailing" liability that can surface years after the move. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Employers carry practical burdens here. They must track employee work locations across the vesting period, determine correct state sourcing at each taxable event, and administer withholding and reporting for potentially several states from one vest. Approaches vary: some employers withhold only for the current work state and rely on employees to true up former-state liabilities on their returns, while others allocate withholding across states based on tracked workdays. A few states apply de minimis thresholds before nonresident withholding is required, and reciprocity agreements between certain neighboring states can simplify wage withholding.
