Given the variation, companies with mobile populations often use specialized mobility-tracking systems and coordinate closely with payroll providers. </Advanced>

title: Cost basis & reporting
summary: Brokers report the sale of equity-comp shares on Form 1099-B, but the basis they report often omits the compensation income already taxed through your W-2. Left uncorrected, this causes the same income to be taxed twice; a Form 8949 adjustment fixes it.
text: ## The reporting chain Selling shares acquired through equity compensation generates two documents. Compensation income - the spread taxed at vest, exercise, or a disqualifying disposition - appears in your wages on Form W-2. The later sale of those shares appears on Form 1099-B, which your broker files and sends to you. ## The double-taxation trap The core problem is that these two forms are not reconciled by the broker. Under the cost-basis reporting rules, brokers generally report to the IRS only the amount you actually paid for equity-comp shares - often just the option exercise price or ESPP purchase price. They are not required to include the compensation income that was already added to your W-2. As a result, the basis on the 1099-B is understated. If you simply copy that low basis onto your return, your reported capital gain is inflated by the exact amount already taxed as wages - so the same dollars are taxed twice. This is one of the most common and costly equity-comp filing errors. ## Correcting it on Form 8949 The fix is a basis adjustment on Form 8949. You start with the broker's reported proceeds and reported basis, then adjust the basis upward to your true, full basis: the amount paid plus the compensation income recognized on your W-2. The corrected gain or loss then flows to Schedule D. Brokerage supplemental statements often show the adjusted basis to help, even when the 1099-B itself does not. ## W-2 versus 1099-B Keeping the roles straight matters: the W-2 captures the ordinary compensation element, while the 1099-B captures the capital gain or loss on disposition measured from full basis. Confusing the two is what produces the double count. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Two information returns support basis and holding-period tracking. Form 3921 is issued for each ISO exercise, capturing the exercise date, exercise price, and fair market value at exercise - data needed for both regular tax basis and alternative minimum tax calculations. Form 3922 is issued on the first transfer of stock acquired under a qualified ESPP, capturing purchase-date and grant-date values used to determine the compensation element on a later sale. Neither form reports income by itself. Instead they arm the taxpayer to compute basis correctly, distinguish qualifying from disqualifying dispositions, and support the Form 8949 adjustment that avoids double taxation. </Advanced>

title: Section 409A deferred compensation
summary: Section 409A governs nonqualified deferred compensation, including some equity awards. Options granted at or above fair market value are generally exempt, but discounted options and certain deferrals fall within 409A, and violations trigger immediate income inclusion plus a 20% additional tax and interest.
text: ## What 409A covers Section 409A regulates nonqualified deferred compensation - broadly, a legally binding right to compensation in one year that is or may be paid in a later year. Its aim is to limit discretion over the timing of income. Although often associated with executive deferral plans, 409A also reaches certain equity arrangements, which is why it matters throughout equity-comp design. ## The stock-option exemption Most stock options are structured to fall outside 409A. An option on the employer's common stock is exempt when its exercise price is at least the fair market value of the underlying stock on the grant date, the number of shares is fixed, and it carries no additional deferral feature. This exemption is why setting an accurate grant-date fair market value is so important - particularly for private companies, which obtain independent 409A valuations to support the strike price. ## When equity falls inside 409A Trouble arises when an option is granted at a discount to fair market value: the built-in spread is treated as deferred compensation and the option becomes subject to 409A. Certain RSU structures can also be caught - for example, when settlement can be deferred beyond vesting rather than paid promptly. In those cases the award must satisfy 409A's rules on election timing and payment events. ## Permissible timing For amounts inside 409A, payment may generally be made only on specified permissible events: a fixed date or schedule, separation from service, death, disability, a change in control, or an unforeseeable emergency. Deferral elections must be made before the compensation is earned, and accelerating payment is broadly prohibited. <Advanced> ## Professional detail The penalties for a 409A failure fall on the service provider, not the employer, and are severe. On a violation, all deferred compensation under the arrangement that is vested becomes includible in income immediately, regardless of whether it has actually been paid. On top of ordinary income tax, the individual owes a 20% additional federal tax on the includible amount, plus a premium interest charge computed as if the income had been recognized when it first vested. Several states layer their own additional tax on 409A violations. Because the consequences are so punitive and land on employees, companies invest heavily in compliant plan documents, defensible grant-date valuations, and disciplined administration of deferral and payment elections. </Advanced>

title: 280G golden parachute
summary: Sections 280G and 4999 discourage oversized payouts to executives tied to a change in control. When such payments reach three times an executive's average pay, a 20% excise tax hits the excess and the company loses its deduction. Accelerated equity vesting counts, and private companies can cure the problem with a qualifying shareholder vote.
text: ## The purpose of 280G Sections 280G and 4999 were enacted to curb outsized compensation triggered by corporate takeovers. Rather than banning such payments, the rules impose tax penalties that make very large change-in-control payouts costly for both the executive and the company, aligning deals more closely with shareholder interests. ## The 3x threshold The rules target "disqualified individuals" - generally officers, highly compensated employees, and significant shareholders. Payments contingent on a change in control are compared to the individual's "base amount," which is average annual W-2 compensation over the five years preceding the change-in-control year. If the aggregate contingent payments equal or exceed three times the base amount, the arrangement crosses into golden-parachute territory. ## Excess parachute payments and the penalties Once triggered, the tax falls on the "excess parachute payment," measured as the amount above one times the base amount (not merely the amount above 3x). Two consequences follow: the recipient owes a 20% excise tax under Section 4999 on the excess, in addition to regular income tax, and the company permanently loses its tax deduction for that same excess. The penalty is therefore doubled-edged, hitting employee and employer at once. ## Equity acceleration Equity is central to 280G analysis. When a deal accelerates vesting of stock options or RSUs, the value linked to that acceleration is generally counted as a parachute payment. Because acceleration can be large, it frequently determines whether an executive breaches the 3x threshold. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Private companies have a relief mechanism unavailable to public companies: the shareholder cleansing vote. If more than 75% of the disinterested shareholders approve the parachute payments after adequate disclosure, and the affected individual waives any excess amount contingent on that approval, the payments can escape 280G treatment entirely. Public companies cannot use the cleansing vote, so they manage exposure through plan design, valuation of accelerated equity, and sometimes contractual "best-after-tax" cutbacks that reduce payments to just below the threshold when that leaves the executive better off. Some agreements historically provided gross-ups - the company paying the executive enough extra cash to neutralize the 4999 excise tax - but shareholder and governance pressure has made gross-ups rare in modern arrangements. </Advanced>

title: Grant-date fair value
summary: Under ASC 718, equity awards are measured at their fair value on the grant date, and that amount fixes the total compensation cost for most awards. Options and similar instruments are valued with an option-pricing model, while full-value awards such as RSUs start from the share price.
text: ## Measuring fair value at the grant date ASC 718 requires share-based payments to employees to be measured at fair value on the grant date, the point at which the employer and employee reach a mutual understanding of the award's key terms and the employer becomes contingently obligated to issue shares. For equity-classified awards, this grant-date measurement is definitive: the resulting amount establishes the total compensation cost, which is then attributed to expense over the service period and is not adjusted for subsequent movements in the share price. The measurement approach depends on the instrument. Full-value awards such as restricted stock units are generally valued at the market price of the underlying share on the grant date, reduced by the present value of any dividends the holder will not receive during the vesting period. Stock options and stock appreciation rights, which have no intrinsic value at grant when issued at the money, must be valued with an option-pricing model because their worth derives from the possibility of future appreciation. ## Option-pricing models and their inputs Two families of models are used in practice. Closed-form models, most commonly Black-Scholes-Merton, produce a single value from a fixed set of inputs and suit straightforward options. Lattice (binomial) models step through time and can accommodate assumptions that change over the option's life, dynamic early-exercise behavior, and vesting that occurs in tranches. ASC 718 permits either, provided the model is consistent with fair-value measurement principles and reflects the award's substantive terms. The principal inputs are the expected term (the period the option is expected to remain outstanding, which is shorter than the contractual term because employees tend to exercise early), expected volatility of the share price, the risk-free interest rate drawn from the government yield curve for a matching horizon, and the expected dividend yield. The exercise price and current share price complete the set. Each assumption must be supportable; the SEC staff has offered guidance on estimating expected term and volatility, particularly for companies with limited trading history. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Expected volatility may be estimated from historical share-price volatility, implied volatility from traded options, or a blend, with the estimation period generally matched to the expected term. Newly public or thinly traded companies often reference a peer group of comparable public companies. For awards with market conditions, a Monte Carlo simulation projects many possible price paths and averages the resulting payoffs, embedding the probability of achieving the condition into a single grant-date fair value. That value is expensed over the derived or explicit service period regardless of the eventual outcome, so no reversal occurs if the market target is missed once service is complete. Nonvested full-value awards carrying a right to nonforfeitable dividends are valued without the dividend-yield reduction, since the holder economically receives those distributions. </Advanced>

title: Expense recognition & forfeitures
summary: Compensation cost for an equity award is recognized over the period the employee must work to earn it. Companies choose how to attribute cost across tranches and whether to estimate forfeitures in advance or record them only when they happen, and performance awards require ongoing probability judgments.
text: ## Recognizing cost over the service period ASC 718 attributes the grant-date fair value of an equity award to expense over the requisite service period, the period during which the employee must provide service to earn the award. In most cases this equals the stated vesting period. The total cost recognized is based only on awards that ultimately vest, so the pattern of recognition and the treatment of departures both matter. For an award that vests all at once (cliff vesting), cost is simply recognized on a straight-line basis over the single period. Complexity arises with graded vesting, where an award vests in successive annual tranches, because later tranches carry a longer service requirement than earlier ones. ## Attribution methods and forfeitures Two attribution methods exist for graded awards that vest based solely on service. Under the straight-line method, total compensation cost is spread evenly across the entire vesting period, subject to a floor: cumulative expense at any date must be at least the fair value of the tranches that have vested. Under the graded (accelerated) method, drawn from FIN 28, each tranche is accounted for as though it were a separate award with its own vesting period, which pushes more expense into the early years. Awards with performance conditions must use the graded approach. For forfeitures, ASU 2016-09 lets a company elect its policy for service conditions. It may estimate expected forfeitures up front, reducing recognized cost accordingly and truing up as actual experience emerges, or it may account for forfeitures only as they occur, recognizing full cost and reversing amounts for unvested awards when an employee leaves. The estimate-based approach smooths expense; the as-incurred approach is simpler but more volatile. ## Performance conditions When vesting depends on a performance condition, such as achieving an earnings or operational target, expense is recognized only if the outcome is considered probable. Management assesses probability each reporting period and recognizes cost for the number of awards expected to vest. If the assessment changes, a cumulative catch-up (true-up) adjusts expense to reflect the revised estimate. <Advanced> ## Professional detail A performance condition affects whether and how many awards vest, so a change from probable to not-probable reverses previously recognized cost entirely. This contrasts sharply with a market condition, which is embedded in grant-date fair value and never reversed once service is rendered. The straight-line floor prevents under-recognition: even though cost is spread evenly, the balance sheet liability or additional paid-in capital must reflect the value of tranches already earned, so recognized cost can never lag the vested portion. When forfeitures are estimated, the true-up mechanism ensures that final cumulative expense equals the fair value of awards that actually vested, matching the outcome under the as-incurred policy while smoothing the interim recognition. </Advanced>

title: Modifications
summary: A modification is any change to the terms or conditions of a share-based award, such as repricing underwater options or accelerating vesting. ASC 718 measures the incremental fair value created by the change and adds it to any remaining unrecognized cost, with the accounting depending on whether the award was expected to vest before and after.
text: ## What a modification is Under ASC 718, a modification is any change to the terms or conditions of a share-based payment award. Common examples include repricing options whose exercise price sits above the market price (underwater options), extending an exercise window, adding or removing a performance target, changing the number of shares, or accelerating vesting when an employee departs. The framework treats a modification as an exchange of the original award for a new one, and the guiding principle is that total recognized cost should never fall below the original grant-date fair value of the award, so long as the employee ultimately vests. ASU 2017-09 narrowed when modification accounting is required. If a change leaves the award's fair value, vesting conditions, and equity-versus-liability classification all unchanged, the company need not apply modification accounting. Any change to one of those three attributes triggers the full analysis. ## Measuring incremental cost The core mechanic is incremental fair value: the fair value of the modified award measured immediately after the change, less the fair value of the original award measured immediately before, both on the modification date. This incremental amount is added to the compensation cost still to be recognized under the original terms. Crucially, a modification cannot reduce cost, if the change lowers fair value, the company continues to recognize at least the original grant-date amount. Timing of the incremental cost depends on vesting status. For an award already vested at the modification date, the incremental value is recognized immediately. For an unvested award, it is recognized over the remaining requisite service period alongside the unrecognized original cost. ## The four modification types ASC 718 organizes outcomes by whether vesting was expected before and after the change. A Type I (probable-to-probable) modification involves an award expected to vest both before and after; incremental fair value is added to original cost. A Type II (probable-to-improbable) modification, such as adding a demanding performance target, means the company recognizes cost based on the original fair value only if the original conditions are met. A Type III (improbable-to-probable) modification revives an award not expected to vest, and cost is based on the modified award's fair value. A Type IV (improbable-to-improbable) modification uses the modified fair value but recognizes cost only if the modified conditions are ultimately satisfied. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Acceleration of vesting on termination is a modification: if the accelerated shares would otherwise have been forfeited, the company recognizes the award's fair value at that date as incremental cost, because service that had not been rendered is being credited. For repricing programs, exchanging underwater options for a smaller number of new options or for RSUs is still analyzed as a modification, comparing the fair value of what is given up with the fair value of what is granted on the exchange date. Type II and Type IV outcomes carry reversal risk: because cost recognition hinges on conditions being met, a company can end up recognizing only original cost, or nothing, if the relevant conditions fail, even though incremental value was created. </Advanced>

title: EPS & dilution
summary: Equity awards affect earnings per share. Basic EPS uses only outstanding shares, while diluted EPS adds the potential shares from options, SARs, and stock units using the treasury stock method. Antidilutive awards are excluded, and awards contingent on performance are counted only once their conditions are met.
text: ## Basic versus diluted EPS ASC 260 requires companies with public stock to present two earnings-per-share figures. Basic EPS divides income available to common shareholders by the weighted-average number of common shares actually outstanding during the period. Diluted EPS expands the denominator to include the additional shares that would exist if all dilutive potential common shares, such as outstanding options, stock appreciation rights, restricted stock units, and convertible instruments, were converted into common stock. The purpose is to show shareholders the maximum potential dilution of their ownership. Equity compensation is a principal source of potential common shares. Because these instruments can increase the share count without a proportional increase in income, they generally reduce diluted EPS relative to basic EPS. ## The treasury stock method For options and SARs, ASC 260 prescribes the treasury stock method. The method assumes that the instruments are exercised at the start of the period (or issuance date, if later) and that the company uses the assumed proceeds to repurchase its own shares at the average market price for the period. Only the net increase, shares deemed issued on exercise minus shares deemed repurchased, is added to the diluted denominator. Assumed proceeds comprise the exercise price the holder pays plus the average amount of unrecognized compensation cost that has not yet been expensed. Including unrecognized cost reflects that the company still receives value in the form of future services. When the exercise price plus unrecognized cost exceeds the average market price, the calculation would add shares that increase EPS, an antidilutive result, so those awards are simply excluded. ## Antidilution and contingent shares An instrument is included in diluted EPS only if it is dilutive, meaning it reduces EPS or increases loss per share. In a net-loss period, all potential common shares are antidilutive and excluded, so basic and diluted EPS are equal. Awards are tested individually, and management may not include antidilutive instruments to smooth results. Performance-based awards raise a timing question. Contingently issuable shares, such as PSUs, enter the diluted calculation only when the contingency would be met if the measurement date were the end of the reporting period. Participating securities that carry nonforfeitable dividend rights require the two-class method, which allocates earnings between common stock and those securities before computing EPS. <Advanced> ## Professional detail The two-class method treats participating securities, for example nonvested restricted stock with nonforfeitable dividends, as a separate class of equity. Undistributed earnings are allocated to common and participating shares according to their respective participation rights, reducing income attributable to common shareholders for both basic and diluted EPS. Diluted EPS uses a year-to-date weighting that considers dilution for each interim period; the annual figure is not simply the sum or average of quarters, and antidilutive quarters cannot offset dilutive ones. Because unrecognized compensation cost declines as awards vest, the assumed proceeds for a given option shrink over time, so the same award typically becomes more dilutive in later periods. </Advanced>

title: SEC registration, Rule 701 & Form S-8
summary: Offering stock or options to employees is an offer of securities, so it must either be registered with the SEC or fit an exemption. Private companies typically rely on Rule 701, while public companies register plan shares on Form S-8.
text: ## Why equity compensation is a securities matter Stock options, restricted stock, RSUs, and shares purchased through an ESPP are all securities. Section 5 of the Securities Act of 1933 makes it unlawful to offer or sell a security through interstate commerce unless a registration statement is in effect or an exemption is available. Granting equity to employees is treated as an offer and sale, so every equity program must rest on either registration or a specific exemption. This is separate from the tax rules that govern the same awards. ## Rule 701 for private companies Rule 701 is the workhorse exemption for privately held companies that do not report to the SEC. It permits sales of securities under written compensatory benefit plans or contracts to employees, directors, officers, general partners, and certain consultants and advisers. The amount of securities that may be sold in any 12-month period is capped by a formula tied to the greater of a fixed dollar figure, a percentage of total assets, or a percentage of the outstanding class of securities. When aggregate sales in a 12-month period stay below the enhanced-disclosure threshold (currently $10 million), the company generally must provide only a copy of the plan. Once sales cross that threshold, the company must deliver richer disclosure to all Rule 701 recipients in that period, including risk factors and financial statements dated within a set recency window. Rule 701 is a federal exemption only; state blue-sky requirements still apply. ## Form S-8 for public companies A company that reports under the Exchange Act uses Form S-8 to register shares issued under its equity plans. Form S-8 is a short-form registration available only to eligible reporting companies that are current in their periodic filings. It covers offers and sales to employees, directors, and consultants who provide bona fide services, but it may not be used to raise capital or to register resales by a broad public group. A company files S-8 to cover the pool of shares reserved under a plan and files additional S-8s as the pool grows. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Rule 701's cap uses the greatest of three measures over a rolling 12-month look-back: a fixed dollar amount, a percentage of the issuer's total assets, and a percentage of the outstanding amount of the class being offered. Options are counted at grant based on the exercise price, not at exercise. The enhanced-disclosure obligation is a condition of the exemption. If the company crosses the threshold but fails to deliver the required information, the exemption can be lost for the entire offering, exposing the issuer to rescission rights. Form S-8 automatically incorporates the issuer's Exchange Act reports by reference, so the prospectus is delivered through a plan document and the company's ongoing filings rather than a standalone document. Affiliates reselling S-8 shares must still comply with Rule 144. </Advanced>

title: Section 16 & Forms 3/4/5
summary: Section 16 of the Securities Exchange Act requires directors, officers, and large shareholders of public companies to report their holdings and trades in company stock. It also lets the company recover profits from certain short-term round-trip trades.
text: ## Who Section 16 covers Section 16 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 imposes reporting and disgorgement rules on the insiders of a company that has a class of equity registered under the Act. Three categories are covered: directors, officers holding policy-making roles, and beneficial owners of more than 10 percent of a registered class. These reporting persons must keep the market informed of their holdings and transactions in the company's equity, including derivative positions such as options and RSUs. ## Forms 3, 4, and 5 Reporting happens on three forms filed electronically through EDGAR. Form 3 is the initial statement of beneficial ownership; a new insider files it within ten days of becoming subject to Section 16 (or by the effective date of registration for a company going public). Form 4 reports changes in ownership and is due by the end of the second business day after most transactions, including grants, exercises, purchases, sales, and gifts in many cases. Form 5 is an annual report covering transactions that were exempt from Form 4 reporting or that were inadvertently omitted, and it is due within 45 days after the company's fiscal year end. ## Short-swing profit recovery Section 16(b) allows the company to recover any profit an insider makes by matching a purchase and a sale (in either order) of company equity within any period shorter than six months. The rule is mechanical: the highest sale price is matched against the lowest purchase price in the window to produce the maximum recoverable profit. There is no requirement to prove the insider used confidential information, which is why insiders and their advisers watch the six-month window closely around equity grants and exercises. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Beneficial ownership under Section 16 is defined by rule and can reach shares held indirectly through family members or entities where the insider has a pecuniary interest. Derivative securities are reported separately, and many grant and vesting events qualify for exemptions under Rule 16b-3 when approved by the board or an appropriate committee. The two-business-day Form 4 deadline was tightened by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. Late filings are disclosed in the company's proxy statement, and a pattern of delinquencies can attract SEC enforcement. Short-swing matching under 16(b) is enforced by the company or, more often, by a shareholder suing derivatively. Exempt transactions such as qualifying grants generally are not matchable, so proper board approval of grants is a key defense. </Advanced>

title: 10b5-1 plans & blackout windows
summary: SEC Rule 10b5-1 provides an affirmative defense against insider trading liability for trades made pursuant to a written plan established when the trader was not aware of material nonpublic information. Blackout windows restrict trading by insiders around earnings releases and material corporate events. Administrators must maintain a blackout calendar and ensure that option exercises, RSU vesting-related sales, and ESPP purchases comply with these restrictions.
text: ## What Rule 10b5-1 does Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and SEC Rule 10b-5 prohibit fraud and manipulation in securities trading. In 2000, the SEC adopted Rule 10b5-1 to address a specific question: when is a person deemed to have traded "on the basis of" material nonpublic information (MNPI)? The rule established a two-part framework. First, it defined "aware of" MNPI broadly: a person trades on the basis of MNPI if they are aware of it at the time of the trade, even if the MNPI was not a but-for cause of the trade. Second, it created an affirmative defense: a person does not trade on the basis of MNPI if they entered into a trading plan when they were not aware of MNPI, and the trades occurred pursuant to that pre-established plan. This affirmative defense allows corporate insiders to set up a written plan for future sales at a time when they are not in possession of MNPI - typically during an open trading window - and then execute those sales automatically at a later time, potentially during a blackout period, without insider trading liability. ## Elements of a valid 10b5-1 plan For the affirmative defense to apply, the trading plan must satisfy all of the following requirements under Rule 10b5-1(c)(1): **Not aware of MNPI at adoption.** The person must have adopted the plan in good faith when they were not aware of any MNPI about the company or its securities. **Specific trading parameters.** The plan must specify (a) the amount of securities to be purchased or sold, (b) the price at which to purchase or sell, and (c) the date of the transaction - or provide a written formula for determining these terms. **No further influence.** Once the plan is established, the person cannot exercise any influence over the timing, amount, or price of trades under the plan. **Good faith and not a scheme.** The plan must be entered into in good faith, not as part of a scheme to evade insider trading prohibitions. ## The 2023 amendments: significant changes The SEC adopted significant amendments to Rule 10b5-1 effective February 27, 2023, in response to academic research and congressional concern that the rule was being abused through short-term plans and plans adopted shortly before material announcements. ### Cooling-off period The most operationally significant change was a mandatory cooling-off period. For Section 16 officers and directors: - The first trade may not occur until the **later of** 90 days after plan adoption or the **first trading day after the company's next quarterly earnings announcement** - subject to a maximum of 120 days. For all other persons: - A cooling-off period of at least **30 days** applies. This effectively eliminates short-term plans designed to execute trades within a few weeks of adoption. ### Single-trade plans Persons may only adopt one single-trade plan per 12-month period. A plan specifying a single transaction is a "single-trade plan." ### Multiple overlapping plans A person may not maintain multiple overlapping 10b5-1 plans with different brokers for the same class of securities, with a narrow exception for plans at two different brokers as long as only one plan is active at a time. ### Certifications Officers and directors must now certify in writing at the time of plan adoption that: (1) they are not aware of MNPI, and (2) the plan is being adopted in good faith and not as part of a scheme to evade insider trading prohibitions. ## Blackout windows A blackout window is a company-imposed period during which employees and insiders are prohibited from trading in company securities. Blackout windows exist independently of Rule 10b5-1 and are typically set by the company's insider trading policy. ### Standard blackout periods Most public companies impose a blackout period beginning shortly before the end of each fiscal quarter and ending 48 hours to two business days after the quarterly earnings announcement. This reflects the period when employees most likely have access to material financial information that has not yet been publicly disclosed. ### Event-specific blackouts Companies may impose ad hoc blackouts around specific corporate events: pending mergers and acquisitions, major product announcements, regulatory decisions, or significant litigation. These blackouts are typically communicated only to affected employees (those involved in the transaction) to avoid tipping the market. ### Equity award considerations during blackouts Administering equity compensation during blackout periods requires careful attention: - **Stock option exercises:** Cashless exercises require market sales, which are restricted during blackouts. Employees with expiring options may need to use a cash exercise or wait for the blackout to lift. 10b5-1 plans can address this for known expiration dates. - **RSU vesting:** Scheduled net-share withholding by the company on vesting dates is generally not considered a voluntary trade and can proceed during blackouts. However, any voluntary sale of vested RSU shares by the participant must comply with the blackout. - **ESPP purchases:** The purchase at the end of an offering period is the company's automatic purchase using accumulated deductions - generally not treated as a voluntary trade and typically proceeds even during blackouts. ## Maintaining a blackout calendar Administrators should maintain a rolling blackout calendar and communicate it to all employees subject to the policy. Best practices include: - Sending an email to covered employees before each quarterly blackout opens. - Providing a second notice before each blackout closes. - Maintaining a list of individuals who are "always-on" insiders subject to year-round restrictions. - Documenting pre-clearance requests and approvals for trades during open windows. - Reviewing option expiration dates well in advance to identify options that may expire during a blackout, so affected employees can plan accordingly.

title: Proxy & executive compensation
summary: Public companies must disclose how they pay their top executives in the annual proxy statement (DEF 14A). Required elements include the Summary Compensation Table, a narrative discussion of pay decisions, a shareholder advisory vote on pay, and pay-versus-performance and pay-ratio disclosures.
text: ## The proxy statement and executive pay Section 14(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 governs how public companies solicit shareholder votes. The definitive proxy statement, filed as a DEF 14A on Schedule 14A, is the primary vehicle for disclosing executive compensation. Item 402 of Regulation S-K sets out exactly what must appear, focused on the company's named executive officers. Because equity awards are a large part of senior pay, the proxy is where equity-compensation practices become most visible to investors. ## Core disclosure tables and narrative The centerpiece is the Summary Compensation Table, which reports each NEO's salary, bonus, stock and option awards, non-equity incentive pay, changes in pension value, and other compensation for the last three fiscal years. Supporting tables show grants of plan-based awards, outstanding equity at year end, and option exercises and stock vested during the year. The Compensation Discussion and Analysis, or CD&A, is a narrative explaining the philosophy, objectives, and decision process behind the numbers, including how performance targets tie to pay. ## Dodd-Frank disclosures The Dodd-Frank Act added several shareholder-oriented requirements. Say-on-pay is a periodic advisory vote asking shareholders to approve NEO compensation, accompanied by a vote on how often that vote recurs. Pay-versus-performance disclosure requires a table and discussion connecting compensation actually paid to measures of company performance, such as total shareholder return and net income. The pay-ratio disclosure compares the CEO's total compensation to the median compensation of all other employees. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Equity awards in the Summary Compensation Table are reported at grant-date fair value under ASC 718, which can differ from the amount ultimately realized. The pay-versus-performance table instead uses a "compensation actually paid" concept that adjusts equity values for changes in fair value across the vesting period, so the two figures rarely match. The CD&A must address clawback policies, hedging and pledging practices, and the use of compensation consultants. It is subject to the say-on-pay vote in substance even though the vote is framed around the overall program. Pay-ratio methodology gives companies flexibility in identifying the median employee and allows the use of statistical sampling, but the methodology and any material assumptions must be disclosed so investors can assess comparability. </Advanced>

title: 10-K / 10-Q equity disclosures
summary: Public companies report the accounting effects of stock compensation in their annual 10-K and quarterly 10-Q filings. The financial-statement footnotes describe expense recognized, unrecognized cost still to come, valuation assumptions, and shares available under equity plans.
text: ## Where equity compensation lands in periodic reports Companies that report under the Exchange Act file an annual report on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q. Both include financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP, and stock-based compensation is governed by FASB ASC Topic 718. The most detailed information appears in a stock-compensation footnote, but the expense also flows through the income statement, is added back on the statement of cash flows, and may be discussed in Management's Discussion and Analysis. ## What the footnote discloses The ASC 718 footnote describes each significant equity plan and the types of awards outstanding, such as options, RSUs, and performance shares. It reports total compensation expense recognized for the period and often breaks it down by award type or income-statement line. A key disclosure is the amount of unrecognized compensation cost tied to unvested awards, together with the weighted-average period over which that cost is expected to be recognized. Activity tables typically roll forward the number of awards granted, vested, exercised, forfeited, and outstanding, along with weighted-average exercise prices and grant-date fair values. ## Valuation and plan capacity Because most awards are measured at grant-date fair value, the footnote discloses the valuation approach and the assumptions behind it, including expected volatility, expected term, the risk-free interest rate, and expected dividends. Companies also disclose how many shares remain available for future grants under approved plans, which signals potential future dilution. In MD&A, management may explain trends in stock-compensation expense and how equity programs affect operating results and liquidity. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Under ASC 718, expense for service-based awards is recognized over the requisite service period, usually the vesting period, based on grant-date fair value. Companies may account for forfeitures as they occur or estimate them, and that policy choice is disclosed. Performance-based awards add complexity: expense recognition depends on whether the performance condition is expected to be met, and market conditions are baked into the grant-date fair value rather than trued up. This distinction affects the timing and reversibility of expense. The 10-Q footnote is condensed relative to the 10-K but must update material changes, including new grants, modifications, and shifts in assumptions. Excess tax effects from settlements flow through the income tax provision and can add volatility to the effective tax rate. </Advanced>

title: Year-end IRS filings (W-2, 3921, 3922)
summary: At year end, employers report equity-compensation income to employees and the IRS. Wages from NSOs and RSUs appear on Form W-2, ISO exercises are reported on Form 3921, and initial ESPP share transfers are reported on Form 3922.
text: ## Reporting equity income on Form W-2 Most equity compensation that produces ordinary income is reported on the employee's Form W-2 under the wage-reporting rules of Internal Revenue Code Section 6051. When a nonqualified stock option is exercised, the spread between the fair market value and the exercise price is wage income. It is included in Box 1 (federal wages), in Boxes 3 and 5 for Social Security and Medicare wages subject to the usual limits, and it is separately shown in Box 12 with Code V. RSU vesting and other ordinary-income equity events are similarly swept into the W-2 wage boxes and subject to withholding. ## Form 3921 for ISO exercises Incentive stock options receive special tax treatment, so their exercises are reported on Form 3921 rather than as W-2 wages. Under Section 6039, a company that transfers stock to an employee upon exercise of an ISO files Form 3921 for each exercise. The form records the option grant date, the exercise date, the per-share exercise price, the fair market value per share on the exercise date, and the number of shares. This information supports the employee's alternative minimum tax calculation and the eventual determination of qualifying versus disqualifying disposition. ## Form 3922 for ESPP transfers Form 3922 addresses employee stock purchase plans that qualify under Section 423. When an employee first transfers legal title to shares acquired under such a plan, the company files Form 3922 to report the details needed to compute income and gain on a later sale, including the grant date, purchase date, purchase price, and share values. Like the W-2 and 3921, the recipient copy is generally due by January 31. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Section 6039 requires both furnishing statements to individuals and filing information returns with the IRS. Only the first transfer of legal title after ESPP purchase triggers a 3922; later transfers are not reportable on that form. For ISOs, no income tax is withheld at exercise, but the spread is an AMT preference item in the exercise year even though it is not regular-tax income. Form 3921 gives the employee the data to reconcile regular tax and AMT and to establish basis. Filing deadlines with the government differ from the January 31 recipient deadline. Employers filing many returns must file electronically, and penalties apply for late or incorrect information returns, so year-end equity reconciliation is a significant administrative task. </Advanced>

title: Rule 144 & resale restrictions
summary: Rule 144 is a safe harbor that lets holders resell restricted and control securities without registering the sale. It sets holding periods, and for affiliates adds volume limits, manner-of-sale conditions, and a Form 144 notice.
text: ## The problem Rule 144 solves Shares received through equity compensation are often restricted or control securities that cannot simply be sold into the market. Section 5 of the Securities Act of 1933 requires registration of a sale unless an exemption applies, and Section 4(a)(1) exempts transactions by persons who are not issuers, underwriters, or dealers. Rule 144 is a safe harbor that tells a holder exactly how to resell without being treated as an underwriter, so the Section 4(a)(1) exemption is available. Meeting its conditions removes the registration hurdle for the resale. ## Restricted versus control securities and holding periods Restricted securities are acquired in unregistered transactions, for example shares issued to employees under Rule 701 or in a private placement. Control securities are held by an affiliate of the issuer, typically a director, officer, or large stockholder, and are restricted by the seller's status rather than how they were acquired. Rule 144 imposes a minimum holding period before restricted securities can be resold: six months if the issuer is a reporting company current in its filings, and one year if it is not. The holding period does not restrict an affiliate's resale of shares that were never restricted, but the other affiliate conditions still apply. ## Conditions for affiliate resales An affiliate using Rule 144 faces additional conditions even after the holding period. Sales within any three-month period are capped by a volume formula tied to the greater of a percentage of the outstanding class or average weekly trading volume. Sales must meet manner-of-sale requirements, generally routed as ordinary brokers' transactions, and current public information about the issuer must be available. If the affiliate's planned sales exceed set thresholds, a Form 144 notice must be filed with the SEC. <Advanced> ## Professional detail The volume limitation for an affiliate is generally the greater of one percent of the outstanding shares of the class or the average weekly reported trading volume over a recent four-week window; for many private-company shares only the one-percent test is meaningful. Rule 144 includes tacking rules that can add prior holders' periods to the current holder's in defined circumstances, and it addresses when the holding-period clock resets. Shares held through certain conversions or as a gift may tack the transferor's period. A Form 144 is required when an affiliate intends to sell above the applicable share-count or dollar threshold within three months. The notice is a signal of intent, not an approval, and it must be filed at or before the time the sell order is placed. </Advanced>

title: Plan design & share pool sizing
summary: Designing an equity incentive plan requires balancing competitive grant levels against dilution to existing stockholders. The initial share reserve must be large enough to fund near-term grants but not so large that it generates adverse proxy advisory votes. Key decisions include pool size, evergreen provisions, award mix, per-person limits, and ISO sub-limits.
text: ## The anatomy of an equity incentive plan An equity incentive plan (EIP) is the legal document that authorizes the company to grant equity awards to employees, directors, and consultants. For public companies, it is approved by stockholders and governs all grants until it expires or is replaced. The plan document specifies the pool of shares available, who can receive grants, what types of awards can be granted, the maximum award per person, and the administrative and governance framework. The core design decisions for a plan are: 1. **Share pool size:** How many shares are authorized for issuance? 2. **Award types:** Which award types are permitted (options, RSUs, RSAs, SARs, PSUs)? 3. **Per-person limits:** Maximum shares that can be granted to any one person in a year? 4. **ISO sub-limit:** How many shares are eligible for ISO treatment? 5. **Evergreen provision:** Does the pool automatically refresh each year? 6. **Fungibility:** Do different award types consume shares at the same rate? 7. **Recapture provisions:** Are shares returned to the pool when awards are forfeited, expire, or are cancelled? ## Share pool sizing at IPO Companies going public typically size their equity plan reserve based on several inputs: **Competitive benchmarking:** What do companies at a comparable stage in the same industry typically authorize as a percentage of fully diluted shares? For technology companies, 10 - 12% of fully diluted shares at IPO is a common starting point. **Hiring plan:** How many shares will the company need to recruit and retain employees over the next 12 - 24 months? The CFO and HR team typically model expected grant activity by level and department. **Proxy advisor guidelines:** ISS and Glass Lewis use quantitative models to evaluate whether a plan has "excessive" potential dilution. ISS's Equity Plan Scorecard (EPSC) evaluates plan costs, burn rates, and plan features together. A company that exceeds ISS's acceptable cost threshold will typically receive an "Against" recommendation from ISS on the plan vote, which influences many institutional shareholders. **Shareholder sensitivity to dilution:** Growth-stage companies that grant equity broadly may find investors more tolerant of larger pools, while mature companies with limited grant activity face more scrutiny. ## The fully diluted share count "Fully diluted shares outstanding" typically refers to basic shares plus all shares issuable under outstanding options (using the treasury stock method), outstanding RSUs (at target for PSUs), shares reserved for ESPP, and the requested new shares under the plan being voted on. Some proxy advisory firms use a "potential dilution" denominator that includes the full pool, not just the treasury-stock method count. The plan share request is typically presented to stockholders as a percentage of both basic shares outstanding and fully diluted shares. A request for 10% of fully diluted shares is viewed more favorably than the same request stated as 15% of basic shares outstanding. ## Fungibility ratios Some plans treat different award types as consuming shares at different rates from the pool: - **Full-value awards** (RSUs, RSAs, PSUs) are typically counted as consuming 1.5x or 2x shares from the pool relative to options. This reflects the greater economic value of full-value awards. - **Options and SARs** are typically counted at 1x. For example, if a plan has a 2:1 fungibility ratio, granting 100,000 RSUs consumes 200,000 shares from the plan reserve, while granting 100,000 options consumes only 100,000 shares. ## Share recycling provisions Most modern equity plans include share recycling provisions that return shares to the pool when: - An option expires unexercised or is cancelled - An RSU is forfeited before vesting - An award lapses However, proxy advisors (particularly ISS) scrutinize certain recycling provisions negatively: - **Shares withheld for taxes:** Some plans allow shares withheld for tax withholding on RSU vesting to be returned to the pool. ISS treats this as a liberal recycling provision and scores it negatively. - **Shares used to pay an option exercise price:** Similarly viewed negatively. - **Net exercises:** Shares not actually issued in a net exercise (the "phantom" shares) should not be recycled back into the pool if the company wants a clean scorecard. ## Per-person limits and Section 162(m) Prior to the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, plan per-person limits were essential for qualifying performance awards under Section 162(m) for deductibility. The TCJA eliminated the performance-based exception, making the $1 million deduction limit under Section 162(m) nearly universal for covered employees. Per-person limits still serve governance and proxy-advisor purposes. Plans typically specify an annual per-person limit on the number of shares that can be granted (e.g., 2 million options or 1 million RSUs per person per year) to demonstrate that the plan is not designed to concentrate all awards in a single person. ## Pre-IPO planning: 409A valuations and option pools For private companies, plan design intersects directly with Section 409A. Options must be granted at FMV, which requires a 409A valuation (a formal independent appraisal). The plan pool size is also a factor in 409A valuations because the option pool is included as a dilutive element in the valuation model. Expanding the option pool before a financing round is a common practice because the post-money valuation (which includes the expanded pool) is typically higher than the pre-money valuation, making the dilution from the pool expansion less visible per-share. This is sometimes called the "option pool shuffle."

title: Share reserve & award limits
summary: An equity plan can only grant awards out of a fixed pool of shares approved by shareholders. That pool is governed by counting rules, ISO caps, sometimes per-person or full-value ratios, and metrics like burn rate and overhang that investors watch closely.
text: ## The authorized share pool Every equity incentive plan is anchored to a finite pool of shares that shareholders have approved for issuance. Awards may only be granted while shares remain in that reserve, so tracking the pool is one of the central administrative duties under any plan. The reserve is set in the plan document as an absolute number, and increasing it generally requires a new shareholder vote. Some plans include an evergreen provision that automatically adds shares each year, typically a fixed count or a percentage of the outstanding share count. Evergreen features are more common in newly public companies but tend to draw criticism from institutional investors because they permit ongoing dilution without a fresh approval. ## Counting and recycling rules Not every granted share reduces the pool one-for-one for the plan's life. Share-counting rules define what happens when awards are forfeited, cancelled, or settled net of taxes. Under a liberal ("full") recycling regime, shares from awards that never deliver value return to the pool. Stricter plans prohibit adding back shares withheld to cover the exercise price or tax withholding. Many plans apply a fungible share ratio, charging full-value awards such as restricted stock units against the pool at a higher rate than options or stock appreciation rights (for example, counting each RSU as more than one share). This reflects the greater economic value delivered by a full-value award. ## Per-award and per-person limits To preserve incentive stock option treatment, the plan must cap the total shares issuable as ISOs. Separately, many plans historically imposed per-person annual limits, a practice driven largely by the former performance-based exception under Section 162(m); although that exception was repealed for most public companies, sub-limits still appear for governance reasons. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Listing standards under the NYSE and Nasdaq require shareholder approval before a company adopts an equity compensation plan or materially increases the shares reserved under one, subject to narrow exceptions (such as certain inducement grants and tax-qualified plans). Material revisions include expanding the share pool, adding an evergreen, extending the term, or repricing where the plan did not previously permit it. Proxy advisory firms evaluate a proposed share request against a model that weighs cost (often a shareholder-value-transfer calculation) alongside three-year average burn rate relative to industry peers, plan features (repricing without approval, liberal recycling, single-trigger acceleration, evergreen terms), and grant practices. A request scoring poorly on these factors can trigger an against recommendation. Administrators should reconcile the reserve continuously: subtract gross awards granted, apply the fungible ratio for full-value awards, and add back only those shares the counting rules permit. Misapplying add-backs is a common source of over-issuance risk. </Advanced>

title: Award design trends
summary: Equity award design has shifted decisively from stock options toward RSUs and performance-based units tied to metrics like relative TSR and financial targets. Double-trigger change-in-control vesting, ownership guidelines, and mandatory clawbacks are now standard governance features.
text: ## From options to full-value awards The center of gravity in equity design has moved away from stock options toward restricted stock units and performance-based units. Options only reward participants when the share price climbs above the exercise price, so a flat or declining market can leave them worthless. Full-value awards deliver shares outright on vesting, so they retain value across market cycles, convey a given dollar amount using fewer shares, and are easier for employees to value. Public companies increasingly split executive equity between time-vesting RSUs and performance stock units (PSUs). ## Performance metrics PSUs vest based on the achievement of defined goals over a multi-year period, commonly three years. Relative total shareholder return (TSR) measured against a peer group or index is among the most widely used metrics because it directly links payout to market performance versus competitors. Companies also anchor awards to financial measures such as revenue growth, earnings per share, operating margin, return on invested capital, or cash flow. Some issuers weight several metrics together and set threshold, target, and maximum payout levels. ## Governance features Design now routinely incorporates governance provisions. Double-trigger vesting has become the norm for change-in-control protection, replacing automatic single-trigger acceleration that investors view unfavorably. Stock ownership guidelines require executives to hold shares worth a multiple of salary, and post-vest or post-exercise holding requirements keep them invested for a period. A growing number of programs also embed ESG or human-capital metrics, such as safety, emissions, or workforce goals, typically as a modifier or a small weighted component rather than the primary driver. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Clawback policies moved from voluntary to mandatory. Listing standards adopted under the Dodd-Frank Act require issuers to maintain a written policy recovering incentive-based compensation received by current and former executive officers during the three fiscal years preceding a required accounting restatement, to the extent that pay exceeded what the corrected figures would have supported. Recovery is generally no-fault and applies to compensation tied to financial reporting measures, including performance equity. Award-design choices carry accounting consequences under ASC 718. Awards with market conditions such as relative TSR are valued using a Monte Carlo simulation at grant, and that grant-date fair value is expensed over the service period regardless of whether the market condition is ultimately met. Awards with performance conditions tied to internal metrics are expensed based on the probable outcome, with expense trued up as the estimate of achievement changes. This asymmetry influences which metrics companies select. </Advanced>

title: Benchmarking
summary: Benchmarking compares a company's equity compensation against a defined peer group to gauge competitiveness, usually by percentile positioning. Companies also benchmark dilution measures like burn rate and overhang, mindful of the frameworks proxy advisors apply.
text: ## Purpose and peer group selection Benchmarking places a company's compensation programs alongside a comparison group so the board and its advisers can judge whether pay is competitive, defensible, and aligned with performance. The foundation is the peer group. Companies assemble peers that resemble them in industry classification, revenue, market capitalization, and often employee headcount or geographic footprint, typically bounding the group within a size range around the company itself. A well-constructed group of roughly fifteen to twenty-five peers gives statistically meaningful data while remaining genuinely comparable. ## Competitive positioning Once peers are set, market data is expressed in percentiles. Companies articulate a compensation philosophy that targets each element (base salary, annual incentive, long-term equity, and total direct compensation) to a chosen percentile, most commonly the median. Positioning above median may be justified for sustained outperformance, hard-to-fill roles, or a deliberate strategy to attract talent, while below-median positioning may reflect other rewards such as culture or upside potential. From this analysis companies build grant guidelines that specify target equity values or share counts by job level or grade. ## Dilution benchmarking Beyond individual pay levels, companies benchmark the aggregate cost of their equity programs. Burn rate (annual shares granted as a percentage of shares outstanding) and overhang (outstanding plus available shares relative to the share count) are compared against industry norms. These measures matter both for internal budgeting of the share reserve and for anticipating how investors and their advisers will react to a plan proposal. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Proxy advisory firms apply structured frameworks that companies must anticipate. Institutional Shareholder Services evaluates equity plan proposals through a scorecard that blends plan cost, grant practices (including three-year average burn rate versus industry and index peers), and plan features, with a passing score needed for a favorable recommendation. Glass Lewis applies its own pay-for-performance analysis, comparing the alignment of executive pay and company performance against a self-constructed peer set and assigning a grade. Market data typically comes from published compensation surveys, proxy-statement disclosures of named executive officer pay, and specialized consultant databases. Private companies rely more heavily on survey data segmented by sector and stage, since public proxy comparisons are unavailable. Administrators should document the peer-selection rationale and the data sources in the Compensation Discussion and Analysis, because Regulation S-K disclosure expectations and investor scrutiny both reward a transparent, consistently applied methodology. </Advanced>

title: 409A valuations & fair market value
summary: A 409A valuation is an independent appraisal that sets the fair market value of a private company's common stock, which becomes the minimum exercise price for stock options. Following a safe harbor gives the company a presumption of reasonableness, and valuations must be refreshed at least every twelve months or after a material event.
text: ## Why a 409A valuation exists Private companies have no public market price, yet they must still set a defensible fair market value (FMV) for their common stock before granting stock options. Section 409A of the Internal Revenue Code treats an option granted with an exercise price below FMV on the grant date as a form of deferred compensation, exposing the recipient to harsh tax consequences. A 409A valuation is an independent appraisal that establishes common-stock FMV so the company can price options at or above that figure and keep them outside the deferred-compensation rules. ## The safe harbors The regulations provide safe-harbor methods that, if followed, create a presumption the FMV determination was reasonable, shifting the burden to the IRS to prove otherwise. The most common is the independent-appraisal presumption: a valuation performed by a qualified independent appraiser is presumed reasonable for stock valued as of a date within the prior twelve months, provided no material change has occurred. Additional safe harbors cover valuations set by a binding formula and a specific method for illiquid stock of a start-up corporation valued by someone with adequate knowledge and experience. ## Consequences of underpricing If an option is under-priced and no exception applies, the holder faces income recognition as the award vests, a 20 percent additional federal tax under Section 409A, and possible premium interest, often with state-level penalties on top. Because the burden and cost fall largely on employees, maintaining current valuations is a core compliance obligation for the issuer. <Advanced> ## Professional detail The twelve-month presumption is not a fixed calendar entitlement. A material event, a priced equity financing, a significant acquisition or divestiture, a major shift in projections, or preparation for a liquidity event, can render an existing valuation stale and require a refresh before the anniversary. Companies granting options during a period of rapid change should re-examine FMV more frequently. The 409A appraisal also intersects with financial reporting. The same common-stock value that anchors the exercise price feeds into the grant-date fair value measured under ASC 718 for stock-based compensation expense, though the accounting fair value of an option is derived separately using an option-pricing model. Divergence between a low 409A common-stock value and a higher value implied by a recent preferred financing can attract auditor scrutiny under the "cheap stock" analysis, particularly in the runway before an initial public offering. Incentive stock options carry a parallel requirement: Section 422 conditions favorable ISO treatment on the exercise price being set at no less than FMV on the grant date, determined in good faith, which the 409A appraisal supports. </Advanced>

title: Day-to-day plan administration
summary: Running an equity plan day to day means keeping accurate grant records, processing vesting and exercises on time, and keeping share counts consistent across the cap table platform and the transfer agent. Strong internal controls protect data integrity and support SOX compliance.
text: ## Keeping the plan running accurately Day-to-day plan administration is the operational work that keeps an equity program accurate and defensible. It centers on clean data: every grant must be recorded with the correct grant date, share count, exercise or purchase price, vesting schedule, and award type. Small data errors compound quickly, because equity records feed compensation expense, cap table ownership, and tax reporting. The core recurring tasks are processing new grants after board or committee approval, applying scheduled vesting events, executing exercises and RSU releases, and recording cancellations or forfeitures when employees leave. Terminations deserve particular care: administrators must apply the correct post-termination exercise window, forfeit unvested awards, and update outstanding balances promptly. Adjustments for stock splits, dividends, or corporate transactions must be applied consistently across all affected grants. ## Reconciliation and the system of record A single system of record prevents conflicting numbers. Most companies designate their cap table or equity management platform as authoritative for outstanding awards, then reconcile it against the transfer agent, which maintains the registered share ledger for issued shares. Regular reconciliation, commonly monthly and always at quarter-end, confirms that granted, vested, exercised, forfeited, and outstanding totals agree across systems and tie to payroll and accounting. <Advanced> ## Professional detail For public companies, plan administration operates inside internal control over financial reporting under Sarbanes-Oxley Sections 302 and 404. Controls typically include segregation of duties so that the person entering a grant is not the person approving it, documented review of vesting and exercise batches, and reconciliation sign-offs retained as audit evidence. Equity compensation expense recognized under ASC 718 depends directly on accurate grant-date fair values, vesting assumptions, and forfeiture data, so a data error is also a potential financial reporting error. Information reporting obligations also flow from clean records. IRC Section 6039 requires furnishing information statements to employees and filing with the IRS for incentive stock option exercises and certain ESPP share transfers, so administrators must capture exercise and transfer details as they occur rather than reconstructing them at year-end. Maintaining an audit trail - who changed what, when, and with what approval - is essential both for the annual financial statement audit and for responding to any later inquiry about a specific award. </Advanced>

title: Participant communications
summary: Participant communications cover the documents and messages that employees receive about their equity, from plan documents and grant notices to prospectus delivery and ongoing education. Companies must deliver required disclosures while making clear they do not provide personal tax advice.
text: ## What participants need to receive Participant communications are the bridge between a technical equity plan and the employees who hold awards. The foundational documents are the plan document itself, which sets the rules the board adopted, and the individual grant notice and award agreement, which state the specific terms of each award: type, share count, price, grant date, and vesting schedule. Employees should be able to find these easily, typically through an equity portal that also shows current holdings, vested and unvested totals, and transaction history. Beyond the legal documents, good communication includes plain-language education. Materials might explain the difference between options and restricted stock units, what vesting means, how an ESPP purchase works, and what generally happens at exercise, release, or sale. For employee stock purchase plans, communication is time-sensitive: enrollment windows open and close on set dates, so administrators must announce them early and confirm elections before each offering period begins. ## Disclosures and the advice boundary A recurring theme across all participant messaging is the boundary on advice. The company can and should explain how the plan operates, but it must not tell an individual employee what to do about their taxes or investments. Materials should say plainly that the company does not provide personal tax, legal, or financial advice and that participants should consult their own advisors. <Advanced> ## Professional detail Securities law drives much of the required disclosure. When a public company registers shares issuable under a plan on a Form S-8 registration statement, it must deliver a plan prospectus - the Section 10(a) prospectus - to participants describing the plan and the securities offered, and keep it current as the plan is amended. Private companies commonly rely on Securities Act Rule 701 for compensatory grants; once aggregate sales during a rolling 12-month period exceed the specified threshold, Rule 701 requires enhanced disclosure to recipients, including a summary of material plan terms, risk factors, and financial statements provided a reasonable time before the awards. Statutory plans carry their own communication needs. ESPPs intended to qualify under IRC Section 423 and incentive stock options under Sections 421 through 424 have specific rules on eligibility, holding periods, and disqualifying dispositions that participants should understand, even though the company still avoids individualized advice. Clear, accurate, and timely education reduces confusion and support burden while helping employees appreciate the value of their equity. </Advanced>

title: Job & life events
summary: Equity awards are affected by a wide range of job and personal life events: termination, death, disability, divorce, leave of absence, company mergers, and IPOs. Administrators must know how each event affects vesting, exercisability, and forfeiture of each award type, and must communicate these consequences clearly and promptly to participants.
text: ## Termination events The most frequent equity administration challenge is handling terminations. The treatment of equity upon termination depends on: the type of award, the reason for termination, and the terms of the plan document and award agreement. Administrators must address each terminated employee's awards promptly to avoid missed exercise deadlines, forfeitures, and tax issues. ### Voluntary resignation and involuntary termination (without cause) **Options:** Unvested options are forfeited on the termination date. Vested options typically remain exercisable for 90 days post-termination (for NSOs, as specified in the plan), or three months for ISOs (to preserve ISO status). Options not exercised within the applicable window are cancelled. **RSUs:** Unvested RSUs are forfeited on the termination date. There is no exercise - if the participant leaves before vesting, they receive nothing. Some plans provide prorated vesting through the termination date if the termination occurs mid-vesting-period, but this is not universal. **RSAs:** Unvested shares are subject to repurchase by the company at the original purchase price (typically close to zero for early-stage grants). The company must exercise its repurchase right within a specified period (typically 90 days) or the right lapses. ### Termination for cause Termination for cause results in immediate forfeiture of all awards - vested and unvested - under most plan documents. This includes cancellation of vested options before they can be exercised. Administrators should flag any for-cause designation in the HR system and ensure that the grant system reflects immediate cancellation without a post-termination exercise window. ### Death Upon death, unvested awards typically vest immediately under the plan (if the plan provides for death acceleration) or are forfeited. Vested options extend to 12 months for ISOs (statutory maximum) and whatever the plan specifies for NSOs - often 12 months as well. The estate or beneficiary may exercise vested options during the extended window. Administrators need a documented process for receiving letters testamentary or trust certifications before processing exercises for deceased participants. ### Disability For ISOs, disability terminations extend the post-termination exercise window from 3 months to 12 months under IRC § 422(c)(6). "Disability" for this purpose is defined under IRC § 22(e)(3) as the inability to engage in any substantial gainful activity due to a medically determinable physical or mental impairment expected to last at least 12 months or result in death. This is a narrower definition than many state disability standards, so administrators should confirm the disability meets the IRC definition before applying the 12-month ISO window. For other awards, the plan document's definition of disability controls the treatment, which may be more generous (e.g., full vesting acceleration upon disability). ## Leave of absence ### FMLA leave The Family and Medical Leave Act requires up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave per year for qualifying medical and family reasons. Vesting schedules typically continue during FMLA leave at most companies, though plan documents vary. The period of FMLA leave is generally not a break in service. ### Military leave (USERRA) Under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act, employees on military leave must be treated as if continuously employed for purposes of vesting and other service-based rights. Upon return from military service, the employee must receive any unvested equity that would have vested during the leave period. Administrators should confirm with legal counsel whether and how to implement USERRA make-up vesting. ### Extended personal leave Unapproved personal leave is generally treated as a termination under most equity plans, triggering the standard post-termination treatment. Some plans provide for suspension of vesting during approved personal leaves exceeding a specified duration (e.g., 90 days). Administrators should check plan provisions and confirm the leave classification before modifying grant records. ## Change in control and M&A events ### Share-for-share exchange When the company is acquired in an all-stock transaction, outstanding equity awards are typically converted into equivalent awards for the acquiring company's stock at the exchange ratio. The number of shares and exercise price adjust by the ratio; vesting schedules carry over. ### Cash acquisition In an all-cash acquisition, outstanding equity awards must be settled at close. Vested options are typically cashed out at the acquisition price minus the exercise price. Unvested options may be cancelled (with or without accelerated vesting) or converted to cash bonuses with the same vesting schedule. The specific treatment depends on the merger agreement's equity provisions. ### Double-trigger acceleration Under a double-trigger provision, unvested equity accelerates if the employee is involuntarily terminated (or resigns for "good reason") within a specified period after the change in control (typically 12 - 24 months). Administrators must track terminations in the post-close integration period and process double-trigger acceleration when it applies. ## IPO and direct listing For employees holding double-trigger RSUs, the IPO or direct listing satisfies the liquidity trigger, allowing all previously time-vested RSUs to deliver shares. This can result in a large tax event for employees who have been with the company for several years - all accumulated vested units may settle on or shortly after the IPO date. Administrators should communicate clearly with employees about the timing and tax consequences of the lock-up period and post-IPO vesting deliveries. The typical post-IPO lock-up period is 180 days, during which employees cannot sell. Large RSU deliveries may occur at or shortly after lock-up expiration. ## Divorce and domestic relations orders Equity compensation is typically treated as marital property in most US states, particularly to the extent it was earned or accrued during the marriage. Dividing equity in divorce is complex because: - Vested options and shares can be transferred using a court order, but the company must establish a process for this. - Unvested awards cannot be legally transferred because they depend on future services that only the employee can provide. - Courts often award an "if, as, and when" order: the employee retains the award, and upon each future vesting event, a specified portion of proceeds must be paid to the former spouse. Administrators receiving divorce orders should engage legal counsel to review the order before any transfer or modification of awards.

title: Advisor & broker coordination
summary: Administering equity means coordinating with outside parties: captive brokers who run cashless exercises and same-day sales, transfer agents who maintain the share ledger, and legal, tax, and payroll teams. Reliable data feeds and clear handoffs keep transactions accurate and compliant.
text: ## The parties an administrator coordinates Equity administration rarely happens inside a single company system; it depends on a network of outside parties working from the same data. The most visible is the captive or designated broker, the brokerage the company selects to execute participant transactions.
