The broker runs cashless exercises, in which shares are sold at exercise to fund the exercise price and taxes, and same-day sales for restricted stock unit releases, and it delivers net shares or cash to employees. Because these transactions generate taxable income, the administrator, broker, and payroll must agree on withholding amounts and timing so the company remits the right tax. The transfer agent is the second key partner. It maintains the authoritative register of issued shares, processes issuances when options are exercised or units release, and holds positions in book-entry form. Administrators reconcile the internal equity platform against the transfer agent regularly so outstanding-share figures match. ## Internal teams and data flow Coordination is also internal. Legal and outside counsel handle plan amendments, securities filings, and insider-trading policy; tax reviews withholding and reporting; and payroll processes the compensation income and withholding that equity events create. Clean, automated data feeds between the equity platform, the broker, and payroll reduce manual errors and keep everyone synchronized. <Advanced> ## Professional detail For insiders, broker coordination intersects with securities law. Rule 10b5-1 lets an insider adopt a written trading plan while not aware of material nonpublic information; if it meets the rule's conditions, including the required cooling-off period, it provides an affirmative defense to insider-trading claims for trades executed under it. Setting up such a plan involves the broker, legal, and the insider, and the broker typically executes trades on the predetermined schedule. Section 16 imposes its own timeline: officers, directors, and ten-percent holders must report transactions in company equity, generally on Form 4 within two business days, and are subject to short-swing profit recovery. Brokers and administrators must feed transaction data to whoever prepares these filings promptly so deadlines are met. On the tax side, equity events trigger federal income and employment tax withholding under IRC Sections 3402 and 3121, which the broker facilitates and payroll remits. Well-defined handoffs and reliable feeds among these parties are what make the whole system dependable. </Advanced>

title: Compliance calendar
summary: A compliance calendar tracks the recurring equity-plan deadlines that recur every year: Section 6039 information statements and IRS filings, W-2 reporting, Section 16 insider filings, S-8 registration, trading windows, proxy season, and the annual 409A valuation refresh. Missing a date can mean penalties or lost compliance.
text: ## Why a calendar matters Equity compliance is built on fixed dates, and many of them cluster at year-end and in the spring. A compliance calendar collects these recurring obligations in one place so nothing slips. Because several deadlines carry penalties or affect the validity of grants, administrators typically build the calendar early each year and assign an owner to every item. The first wave hits in winter. Under IRC Section 6039, companies must furnish information statements to employees by January 31 for the prior year: Form 3921 for incentive stock option exercises and Form 3922 for the first transfer of legal title to ESPP shares acquired under a qualified Section 423 plan. The corresponding filings to the IRS are due by February 28 on paper or March 31 if filed electronically. Form W-2, which reports equity compensation income and withholding, is also due to employees by January 31. ## The rest of the year Section 16 filings are event-driven rather than calendar-driven but must be tracked continuously: Form 3 within ten days of becoming an insider, Form 4 generally by the second business day after a reportable transaction, and Form 5 after year-end for certain items. Trading windows open and close around earnings, and any 10b5-1 plans should be logged with their cooling-off periods. Proxy season in the spring drives compensation disclosure, and Form S-8 registrations may need topping up as evergreen share reserves grow. <Advanced> ## Professional detail The annual 409A valuation refresh anchors the private-company calendar. To set incentive stock option and nonqualified option exercise prices at fair market value, companies obtain an independent valuation and refresh it at least every 12 months, and sooner after a material event such as a new financing round or a significant change in the business. A valuation that meets the Section 409A safe-harbor conditions shifts the burden to the IRS to show the value was grossly unreasonable, which protects both the company and optionholders from the substantial taxes and penalties that a below-market exercise price on deferred compensation can trigger. For public companies, the calendar also tracks Form S-8 registration of new plan shares, which must be effective before shares are issued, and the interplay of blackout periods with the equity-transaction schedule. Building buffer time before each statutory deadline, rather than working to the deadline itself, is the practical safeguard that keeps the program compliant year after year. </Advanced>

summary: An ISO is a statutory stock option governed by IRC Section 422 that can only be granted to employees and receives favorable tax treatment when specific holding requirements are met. No regular income tax is due at grant or exercise, though the spread at exercise is an adjustment item for the alternative minimum tax. If the shares are held long enough, the entire gain is taxed as long-term capital gain.

summary: A cliff is an initial period during which no portion of an award vests, followed by a lump vesting event once the cliff is reached. title: Grant date
summary: The grant date is when the company and recipient reach a mutual understanding of the key terms of an award, and the company becomes committed to issue it. The election carries risk because taxes paid are not refunded if the property is later forfeited.

title: Disqualifying disposition

title: Holding period
summary: The holding period is the length of time an asset is owned, which determines whether a gain is short-term or long-term for capital gains purposes. Holding more than one year generally qualifies gains for lower long-term rates. For statutory equity awards, specific holding periods also govern whether favorable tax treatment applies.

title: Capital gains
summary: Capital gain is the profit from selling a capital asset such as stock for more than its cost basis. Gains on assets held longer than one year are taxed at preferential long-term rates, while shorter holdings are taxed as ordinary income. In equity compensation, the capital gain is measured from the basis established when the award was taxed as income.

title: Burn rate
summary: Burn rate is the annual rate at which a company grants equity awards, usually shown as shares granted in a year divided by shares outstanding. It indicates how quickly a company consumes its share reserve. Proxy advisors benchmark burn rate against industry norms when evaluating equity plan proposals.

title: Cost basis
summary: Cost basis is the amount used to measure gain or loss when shares are sold, generally the purchase price plus any income already recognized and taxed. For equity awards, basis usually equals the exercise price or purchase price plus any ordinary income reported at exercise, vesting, or settlement. Accurate basis tracking prevents the same income from being taxed twice.

title: Supplemental wage withholding
summary: Supplemental wages such as equity award income can be subject to a flat federal withholding rate, with a higher mandatory rate applying to amounts above a statutory threshold in a year. Employers apply these rates to income from RSU vesting, NSO exercises, and similar events. Because the flat rate may differ from a person's actual marginal rate, withholding can be higher or lower than the eventual tax.
